Serjeant-at-Arms—Brent Smith

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, most members will be aware that our
Serjeant-at-Arms retires tomorrow, after 13 years in the role. I am sure that members
would join with me in thanking Brent Smith for his service and in wishing him all the
best for a well-earned retirement. [Applause]

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am not applying for the job,
by the way. When the House resumes on Tuesday, 29 Marc h the Government will look
to make progress on the New Zealand Business Number Bill and first readings of the
New Zealand Horticultural Export Authority Amendment Bill and the Wildlife
(Powers) Amendment Bill, and also progress on the Committee stages on t he Order
Paper.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Mr Speaker, can I just, on behalf of
the Opposition and in keeping with the statement you made at the beginning of question
time today, add our thanks to Brent Smith for his 13 years of service to the House. I am
told that in that time, he has taken only 1½ days of sick leave. So I hope that his
successor will have a similar level of dedication and commitment to this House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member.
Prime Minister, Statements—New Zealand Women Leaving for Syria and Iraq
1. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister : Was he
advised, prior to 8 December 2015, that the so called “jihadi brides” he referred to
during the Intelligence and Security Committee meeting were a ll resident in Australia
and did not leave from New Zealand?
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House)  on behalf of the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: So the Prime Minister can confirm that he knew that none of those
women had left for Syria or Iraq from New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, and the member needs to be aware that as New
Zealand citizens it does not matter where they left from . If they pose a security risk to
New Zealand on their return, then that is something we are concerned about.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister not make it clear that these women did
not leave from New Zealand when he said: “There’s , in my view, no question that there
have been one or two people who have left and it would appear on all factors that we
know that they are going as jihadi brides.”?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It was not actually the Prime Minister who answer ed
the question, but what I can say is that where they leave from is irrelevant. They are
New Zealand citizens, they may return to New Zealand, and they are of concern to us.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister not tell New Zealanders  that these
women were living in Australia when the media were reporting that these women had
left from New Zealand?
9868 Oral Questions 17 Mar 2016

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am unware of the media reports and not responsible
for them. The reality is that they were travelling on New Zealand passports.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: If the Prime Minister knew that no women had left from New
Zealand for Syria or Iraq for this purpose, why did he not give that information to the
Islamic Women’s Council, which asked for evidence for his statements?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Where they left from is irrelevant. If they are New
Zealanders then they are of concern to us. If they are posing a security risk because they
may return to New Zealand, that is of concern to u s. Whether someone is in New
Zealand or not does not remove their New Zealand citizenship —as we have recently
found out.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was very clear:
why did the Prime Minister not give information to an organisation when they asked for
it? It was irrelevant—his answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, no, but the question was addressed by the Minister —
effectively, saying that where they left from was irrelevant. That was the way he chose
to answer the question. He has addressed the question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister allow the misinformation about where
these women were living to carry on, and was it because he was wanting to build his
case for increased spy agency powers?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No, the fact is that these women are New Zealand
citizens, have travelled to Syria, and may pose a security risk to New Zealand on their
return.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Prime Minister now ap ologise to the many Muslim
women—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question can be asked.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Prime Minister now apologise to the many Muslim women
whom he alienated when he misled the public into believing that women were leaving
New Zealand to become jihadi brides?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: No, because there is only one person in this House
who has identified these people as being Muslim. I will make the other point that New
Zealand citizens on a New Zealand passport going to Syria from another country left
New Zealand at some point.
Economy—Reports
2. CHRIS BISHOP (National) to the Minister of Finance: What recent reports has
he received on the New Zealand economy?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : Statistics New Zealand has today reported that the ec onomy grew 0.9
percent in the 3 months to December. This took annual growth over 2015 to 2.3 percent.
The first half of 2015 was a weaker time for the economy, so it is pleasing to see that
growth has picked up again in the second half of the year, with tw o quarters of nearly 1
percent growth now. Growth was led by service industries, which made up 70 percent
of the economy. The construction sector also saw strong growth. Our 0.9 percent
growth rate compares positively with other developed countries, with 0 .6 percent in
Australia, 0.5 percent in the UK, and 0.3 percent in the US. The OECD average was 0.3
percent.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How is diversification of the economy contributing to sustained
moderate growth and delivering more jobs and higher in comes for New Zealand
families?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is clear from these numbers that the New Zealand
economy is proceeding in a diversified manner. We have a dairy industry that is having
17 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9869
a difficult time at the moment, but, despite thi s, we are seeing solid growth, more
employment, and higher wages. Although we are, of course, concerned for dairy
farmers, the important lesson is that it does not mean that the whole economy is in
difficulty. And that, frankly, is a good thing for all of New Zealand. We are seeing
continued growth across many parts of the economy. For example, tourism is
performing well; annual beef exports are now up one -third in the last year; international
education was worth $3.1 billion in 2015 —and that supports 30,00 0 jobs —and wine
exports are now worth $1.5 billion, up 14 percent in just 1 year.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Do the latest GDP figures show the second consecutive quarter of
falling per capita real disposable income?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN J OYCE
items.text: I congratulate the member, because he has obviously been
in his office trying to find the one slightly negative statistic, ever since quarter to 11 this
morning. Real GDP per capita, which the member used to care about, up until this
week, has gone u p in both of the last two quarters. The real gross national disposable
income per capita, which the member is now so fixed on, has gone down slightly in the
latest figures.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Was Westpac senior economist Michael Gordon wron g when he
said that GDP growth per capita is “actually very sluggish at present.”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Speaking of sluggish—no, it is not. The September quarter
and the December quarter are both at 0.3 or 0.4, from memory.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: So he’s wrong?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, the Westpac economists were predicting 7 percent
unemployment this year at one stage. I note they have been very quiet on that lately.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: What reports has he received recently on reductions in New Zealand’s
external financial vulnerabilities?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is good news there, too. Statistics New Zealand yesterday
released its latest balance of payments figures. They showed a curre nt account deficit of
3.1 percent, which, of course, is significantly better than we used to experience. We
were around the 8 percent mark back in the period prior to the global financial crisis,
before this Government came into office. Statistics New Zealand also reported that New
Zealand’s net external debt has now fallen to 55 percent of GDP, down from 83 percent
when National took office, and is now at the lowest level since 2003. These figures
represent good progress in improving a longstanding imbalan ce in the New Zealand
economy, which we inherited. Lower national debt means New Zealand is better placed
to respond to any future economic shocks.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How is the Government’s responsible and consistent programme of
economic manage ment, which contrasts with reports of other, more knee -jerk
approaches, supporting ongoing moderate growth in the economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is important that the Government continues to undertake
responsible and consistent economic reform that gives businesses the confidence to
invest and grow, and not just react to the latest news cycle. We are doing that, for
example, through the Business Growth Agenda, which includes 350 initiatives, like
signing up to new free -trade agreements, reducing ACC levies by around $1.5 billion a
year, rolling out the ultra -fast broadband programme, and launching three new ICT
graduate schools. This all translates into an outlook that is for continued economic
growth. In fact, Treasury’s Half Year Economi c and Fiscal Update forecast growth
averaging around 3 percent over calendar years 2016 and 2017, while the Reserve Bank
forecast is similar for the next 2 years.
9870 Oral Questions 17 Mar 2016
Dairy Industry—Milk Price Downturn
3. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by his reported statement from February this year that he is not
overly concerned about the broader impact of the slump in dairy prices?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : In the context in which it was made, yes. As I said earlier, there is a
difference between being concerned for farmers, and being concerned that the dairy
sector will drag the rest of the economy into recession. Of course, we have seen that that
will not necessarily happen, because of the GDP figures today. Of course we are
concerned about the welfare  of farmers, but this does not detract from the fact that we
are seeing continued growth across the rest of the economy. Despite the fall in dairy
prices, for example, exports actually increased by almost $2 billion for New Zealand
last year and, as I ment ioned in the earlier question, tourism, beef exports, international
education, and wine are just four examples of that growth.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is Waimate mayor Craig Rowley wrong when he says that the
dairy downturn is going to have a “ massive onflow” in his town and that “There will be
no winners. It’s a struggle for everybody.”, or should the people of Waimate not be
overly concerned, either?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Obviously there are some towns that are being affected by
the downturn in dairy prices. I can think of a number that I have visited in recent times
that are affected on that basis.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: So they should be concerned?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: They of course will be concerne d, because of their local
economic environment. My point to the member, who constantly says that the only
thing in New Zealand is the dairy industry, is that the figures we have now prove that
New Zealand has a diversified economy that is growing well, and  that is actually good
for all those towns, because if we were not growing well at this point they would have
more reason to be concerned.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is AgriBusiness Group economist Stuart Ford wrong when he
says that “The flow on effect for … places like Christchurch are absolutely massive”
from the dairy downturn, or should the people of Christchurch not be overly concerned,
either?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Christchurch economy is New Zealand’s second -
largest, and has a whole range of industries in it.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: So he’s wrong, as well?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Grant, just quieten down for a little bit—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —and wait for your question. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Complete the answer, please.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: My point is that the Christchurch economy is a large
economy that is diversified in areas such as ICT, high -tech manufacturing, construction,
and the food sector more generally, including the meat sector and a whole range of
fisheries production. The Christchurch economy is a strong economy. It will, of course,
be affected to some degree by the dairy downturn, but, as we have s een across New
Zealand as a whole, the New Zealand economy continues to perform well and is one of
the highest performing economies in the OECD, notwithstanding the challenges of the
dairy industry.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answe r, is not what the GDP numbers actually
show is that whatever growth we do have is not sustainable, because it does not come
17 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9871
through increased productivity or output, but rather comes from population increase and
debt-fuelled household spending?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No. The member’s talking points are simply wrong. But
where he has a point is where, if you remove every part of the New Zealand economy
that is growing, you will find that the balance is not growing. It is a bit like a Monty
Python sketch, but if you remove immigration, education, tourism, the wine industry,
the meat industry, the ICT industry, and —for all I know —ethnic restaurants, you will
find that there is no growth in the New Zealand economy.

items.speaker: Fletcher Tabuteau
items.text: Does the Minister not think that his current apathy and silence
on New Zealand dairy farmers opens this Government up to the very reasonable label of
fair-weather friend?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think there are some parties that coul d be called fair -
weather friends of the dairy sector, but it is not this one. The Government is very
involved, and has always been involved, in the dairy sector. Where was the member’s
party on, well, the Trans -Pacific Partnership for a kick -off, irrigatio n, and on
encouragement of the Primary Growth Partnership programme, which encourages the
development and progression up the value chain of the dairy industry. All of these
things this Government has been involved in for a very long time, and I am pleased that
the member is finally turning up with some concern for the dairy industry.
Students with Special Needs—Intensive Wraparound Service
4. STUART SMITH (National —Kaikōura) to the Minister of Education : What
reports has she received on the Intensive Wraparound Service?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. The
Intensive Wraparound Service is a personalised service that supports children and
young people with high and complex behavioural and learning needs. I recently
received the results of a review of this service conducted by the New  Zealand Council
for Educational Research. The review found that it is improving behaviour and
educational outcomes for some of the highest -need children and young people who
receive this service. Additionally, families involved in the study saw the Intens ive
Wraparound Service as a major improvement for their children. Indeed, one family
described it as a “lifesaver”. Introduced in 2012, this service gives parents the choice of
a locally based wraparound service within their local community, and children a nd
young people the support they need to attend their local school.

items.speaker: Stuart Smith
items.text: What other action is she taking to ensure that students with the
highest needs are supported in our education system?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Posi tive Behaviour for Learning is another highly
successful programme. This programme has 10 initiatives to help parents, whānau,
teachers, early childhood centres, and schools to address problem behaviour, improve
children’s well -being, and increase educatio nal achievement. Schools involved with
Positive Behaviour for Learning have reported a dramatic drop in suspensions and
resulting exclusions, and an increase in student achievement. Teachers report that it has
contributed to a more respectful and inclusive  school culture, improved approaches to
addressing behaviour incidents, improved school safety, and a decrease in behaviour
referrals for major incidents. I congratulate families, schools, and communities on their
hard work in making the Intensive Wraparou nd Service and the Positive Behaviour for
Learning initiatives a success.
Work and Income—Client Management System
5. CARMEL SEPULONI (Labour —Kelston) to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: How many applications for benefits, superannuation, and special needs
9872 Oral Questions 17 Mar 2016
grants have not been processed because of the issues with the implementation of the
client management IT system?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am advised that Work
and Income is unaware of any applications for benefits, superannuation, and special
needs grants that have not been processed due to the introduction of the new client
management system. All applications have been processed within normal business -as-
usual time frames, and client applications and payments have been given top priority.
All client services are now operating as usual, and any clients with concerns  should
contact Work and Income.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Is the reason that she cannot provide a number that the booking
system is experiencing serious faults and that staff are unable to edit or load client files
into the client management system?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: No, it is because there are none.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Does she stand by her statement last week that “the system is
continuing to improve, with an expectation of being at full capacity in the next day or
so”; if so, why are there thousands of client files, as of yesterday, still unable to be
called up by Work and Income staff?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am advised that the amount of work on hand is within the
normal range and is being processe d within the expected time frames. All work relating
to payments is being prioritised, the system’s performance has continued to improve
since implementation, and I have received regular updates on the system. One hundred
percent of the staff are now able to use the system, and all client channels are operating
as usual.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Have Work and Income staff had immediate access to the high -
risk client database the entire time since the rollout of the upgrade to the client
management IT system; if not, what security risks has this posed to her staff?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: My understanding is that there were some systems that were
not available for some periods of time, but at all times security of staff is uppermost in
the minds of Work and Income.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: What additional security measures has she put in place to mitigate
the security risks for her staff not being able to identify high-risk clients quickly?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: As I  have already said, any of those services that were not
available were unavailable for only a short period of time. All offices have security
officers in place, and, as I say, especially last week, the security and safety of staff was
uppermost in the minds of all Work and Income managers.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Is she able to guarantee that benefit recipients who are entitled to
the benefit rate increase on 1 April will receive this increase on time?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: My understanding is that all benefit payments will be paid in
accordance with the normal operating practices. I have particularly asked about the
benefit increase from 1 April and I am assured that that will take place, but that does
rely on all the information being available from applicants.
Vote Health—Funding Changes
6. BARBARA KURIGER (National—Taranaki - King Country) to the Minister
of Health: By what percentage has Vote Health increased since 2008?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I am pleased to confirm
that despite tight global financial times since 2008, National has increased  spending on
Vote Health by over 30 percent. This $4 billion increase has supported the expansion of
health services such as free under -13s GP visits, over 5,500 more doctors and nurses,
and 50,000 surgeries, but it has also seen a huge investment in capit al projects, such as
nearly $1 billion on Canterbury’s health infrastructure and the upcoming hospital
17 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9873
rebuilds on the West Coast and in Dunedin. Only National can both manage the books
and increase access to health services.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that under this Government the average
share of the economy invested in Vote Health is 6.5 percent, and how does this compare
historically?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The share of the economy invested i n health is
probably the most widely accepted measure of the priority that the Government of the
day places on health. I can confirm that the average share of the economy invested in
health under National is 6.5 percent, and this is much higher than the av erage 5.7
percent invested in health by Labour from 2000 to 2008.
Forestry—Job Losses and Timber Processing
7. Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour —West Coast - Tasman) to the Minister
for Primary Industries: Does he have confidence in his Associate Minister for Primary
Industries?
Hon JO GOODHEW (Associate Minister for Primary Industries) on behalf of
the Minister for Primary Industries: It is still yes.
Hon Damien O’Connor : Has the Associate Minister raised with the Minister any
concerns about the 6,000 jobs lost across the forestry sector at the same time  that the
harvested volume of logs has increased by 50 percent?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: As when the Minister was the Associate Minister, and also
the Minister with responsibility for forestry, this is an ongoing issue for the forestry
sector. So M inister Goodhew and the Minister have actually discussed this. However,
what we do know is that there are more logs being processed in New Zealand than ever
before. That is of higher value than logs going out. The other thing that this Government
is doing is, certainly, assisting and supporting the log processing sector so that there is a
higher value coming back to New Zealand’s workers.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: What has his Associate Minister proposed to remedy the problem in
Gisborne, where Malaysian-owned Hikurangi Forest Farms refuses to guarantee logs to
a locally owned saw mill, preferring, rather, to export them, even though the mill
owners are prepared to pay export-equivalent log prices?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: It will come as no surpris e to this side of the House, at least,
that this Government is not going to get itself in the middle of a commercial
arrangement. We will not require any owner who is harvesting logs to supply at any
particular cost to any processor.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Can the Minister confirm to the House that logs exported from
New Zealand ports by vertically integrated, foreign -owned forestry companies that own
cutting rights to New Zealand in saw mills overseas actually earn New Zealand
anything in terms of direct net foreign exchange?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Has she expressed any concern at all that Hikurangi Forest Farms may
lose its internationally recognised International Forest Stewardship Council certificatio n
because of its refusal to guarantee the supply of logs to a local saw mill; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Minister Goodhew has not raised that with the Minister.
Tourism—Visitor Numbers and Chinese Tourism
8. BRETT HUDSON (National) to the Minister of Tourism : What reports has he
received about growth in the number of visitors coming to New Zealand?
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Associate Minister of Tourism)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Tourism
items.text: A record 3.2 million tourists visited New Zealand, of course, in
2015. In particular, there has been a huge increase in the number of visitors from China,
9874 Oral Questions 17 Mar 2016
with arrivals for the year ended January 2016 up by 42 percent on the year before. They
are also, of course, spending more, which is great news for us here, with Chinese
visitors’ spending growing even faster than arrival numbers. In 2015 they spent more
than $1.6 billion while visiting New Zealand.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: What are we doing to attract Chinese visitors to New Zealand?
Hon Damien O’Connor: Cheap airfares.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: This side of the House, this Government, is doing a great
job in actually attracting Chinese visitors, and even welcoming Chinese who might want
to stay here on their visas and even work in ethnic restaurants. We kind of encourage
that as well —if the member wants to chirp up there. Es timates show that up to 70,000
people visited during Chinese New Year this year, and we need to do all we can to,
obviously, capitalise on this. Regional tourism organisations are working with officials
to get better insights on what they can do to attract Chinese visitors to their regions.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: What risks are there to the continued growth of Chinese tourism?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Some of the risks that we actually have in the sector are
being able to ensure that we have the right staff and skilled staff working in different
areas, particularly in hospitality —as you can see, actually, by the Tourism Industry
Association New Zealand, which put out a press release. It said it was really concerned
that any ban on oversea s chefs while working in New Zealand would have a disastrous
consequence for the tourism industry and the economy, actually, for the money that
tourism is bringing in. As the quote says: “The policy position taken this week by the
Labour Party leader”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There is no responsibility for that.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that yesterday’s current account figures show that
despite an increase in the number of international visitors to New Zealand in the latest
quarter, total expenditure fell by $57 million?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No.
Youth Employment and Training—Statistics and Immigration
9. RON MARK (Deputy Leader—NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by all his statements where the interests of young New Zealanders are concerned?
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House)  on behalf of the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: Insomuch as they are accurately quoted or reported, yes.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: If the Prime Minister in 2009 said: “We simply can’t afford to leave our
young languishing on a benefit.”, why are there now 37,700 Māori and Pacific Island
youth not in jobs, education, or training?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: We have some of the lowest levels of unemployment
for people in that category in New Zealand’s history. If the member is serious about
supporting young people into  work, then he would support the expansion of the
economy and immediately sign up to the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: How will young New Zealanders access affordable rental homes and
ownership when they face competition from a n et 65,900 migrants a year into New
Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am not at all pessimistic about the future for young
New Zealanders, in a country that is led by a Government that is progressive, that does
want the economy to grow, and  does have an international focus towards the world that
those young people will eventually lead.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Reflecting on his answer to supplementary question No. 1, what on earth
is he doing to help young New Zealanders get ahead, when our rate of young people not
in jobs, education, or training is worse than that of Poland and the Czech Republic?
17 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9875

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The statistic that the member is putting in front of the
House is the lowest it has been in New Zealand’s histo ry, and the whole programme
that this Government is running is about expanding the size of the New Zealand
economy to create the sort of opportunity that those young people will want. But do not
be pessimistic about the whole of the young people who fit in to that neat group. The

12. JENNY SALESA (Labour —Manukau East)  to the Minister for Tertiary

not be proceeding into the teaching profession, but, actually, again, from the

Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It
is not usual for the Minister proposing a bill to speak in the second reading, but this is a
bill that is somewhat unique, and I think it continues the historically strong support that
this Parliament has given Christchurch through the difficult years post the earthquake
sequence—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just ask the member—he needs to move that the bill be
read a second time.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Oh, sorry. Well, there you go. It just shows that
anybody who has been here for any length of time can demonstrate a bit of inexperience
occasionally. I move, That the Greater Christc hurch Regeneration Bill be now read a
second time.
As I was saying, this is, I think, a historic bill for the House, and the events of the last
couple of weeks, where parties have come together to discuss the final shape of the
bill—albeit post the select  committee stage—have been particularly pleasing. I would
like to acknowledge the chair of the Local Government and Environment Committee for
the work that he and his members did on this bill. It was in hearing the submissions that
some of the complexities that needed to be dealt with in the bill were brought to light.
The genesis of the bill, though, started quite some time ago, when it was decided that
there should be an orderly transition for the Government to exit some of its more
prominent roles in th e recovery of Christchurch. So in December of 2014, under the
chair of Dame Jenny Shipley, there was an advisory board set up. It was asked to
consider a number of parameters that should be given a fair old going over before any
transition plan could be pu t together, and then it was asked to produce a report that
would indicate a direction moving forward.
That advisory board had on it the Mayor of Christchurch, the Mayor of Waimakariri
District, the Mayor of Selwyn District, and the current chair of Enviro nment
Canterbury, as well as people from the business sector and a number of people from the
NGO sector, as well. The people who were on that board did, I think, a splendid job of
thinking about the state of the city at present, particularly in a governanc e sense, and
looking at what might be necessary moving forward. So what we have seen in the last
10 days, when MPs have repeatedly met, discussed, and agreed, is a continuation of a
consultation process that has gone on for a very long period of time. The arrangements
that are now going to be presented in the Committee stage as a Supplementary Order
Paper to this particular bill, when the House resumes after the adjournment, I think are
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9879
going to put into statute a series of arrangements that will work well for the future of the
city.
It is particularly pleasing —I will say it again —that we have been able to reach a
broad consensus on how that should shape up, and I would like to take this opportunity
to acknowledge the hard work, and actually the determined work, I should say, of all the
MPs who were party to that. These were Denis O’Rourke from New Zealand First,
Eugenie Sage from the Green Party, Te Ururoa Flavell from the Māori Party, David
Seymour from the ACT Party, Megan Woods from the Labour Party—I think that might
cover it. But my point is that when we were in those discussions, the general perception
of Parliament as being an adversarial place was for a time set aside while there were
proper discussions about what the consequences of any law might be . I have to say that
the bill is not, for example, in a shape that I would think meets in every way the
requirements that I would see necessary, but then I think every other person in the room
would have come up with the same conclusion, and that, I think,  can give us all comfort
that we are probably in about the right space.
The most salient points that have come out of those discussions relate to the
provisions that will go into the Supplementary Order Paper that effectively strengthen
public input into any of the regeneration plans that will be developed in Christchurch
City. It will strengthen the leadership of the new organisation Regenerate Christchurch
and it will put a degree of constraint—a greater degree of constraint—on the exercise of
ministerial powers to alter those plans under clause 42 of the bill.
Those regeneration plans, you could almost say, are a copy of the recovery plan
process that has been in place over the last few years. But, essentially, the bill
recognises that although Christchurch has had its emergency and then has gone through
a period of recovery, and continues to do so, we are now at a point where the
consequences of the earthquakes have made such significant changes to the city and the
greater Christchurch area that sharper processes are going to be necessary to ensure that
we do develop new areas, redevelop existing areas, and renew existing areas in a way
that make them most amenable to people’s ongoing living opportunities. So although
there will be some who look at this and say “You’re replacing one bureaucracy that is
centrally controlled by Government with a whole lot of smaller bureaucracies that are
controlled by local organisations with lesser direct authority.”, I think that they have
missed the point that there are  some very separate considerations that need to be put in
place.
So Regenerate Christchurch becomes the prime body for taking an overview of the
city and its surrounds and making determinations about where some of the efforts of
local authorities, individual developers, and others who have an interest in an area can
be concentrated, and then coming up with plans that will enable that to occur on a much
more rapid basis than might occur through the Local Government Act or, for that
matter, some aspects of the Resource Management Act.
Then you have an organisation that the council is setting up called Development
Christchurch Ltd. That is designed to be a front -face, first point for people who are
coming to the city who want to invest. One of the things that I hear over and over, and
have done for the last few years, is that people come into town and say “Right, we want
to do something.”, and then there is nowhere to go, no one to talk to, and nothing gets
done. I think that is an overstatement of how things are, but the council certainly does
have a desire to see things move. I think the first thing that Development Christchurch
has been involved in is the big bike park on the Port Hills, which the rest of the country
will soon learn is an absolute ly splendid facility, and I am sure there will be many who
come to Christchurch because of it.
9880 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
There is also going to be an organisation referred to as Ōtākaro Ltd. Everyone will
know that the Government has invested heavily in Christchurch. It does own a  lot of
land known as the red zone and does own a lot of land in the central business district,
where the different precincts are being established. It will hold the interest that the
Government has in ensuring that the anchor projects that remain —at this point—
unstarted are started and that those that are under way continue to their completion at as
speedy a pace as possible.
We have cross-pollinated all of those boards with the chairs of each so that there is a
good understanding and good working arrange ment between those groups. I think the
structure recognises local autonomy and recognises the difference between a single
body that does everything and the specifics that need to be dealt with, and I am
confident that they will be able to work together in a very, very positive way.
This is, as I said before, a historic bill. It is part of the efforts that this Parliament is
making in support of Canterbury, and it continues the unanimous support and generous
support that the House has given since the days p ost-2011. The discussion that we will
have in the Committee stage will make very clear, I hope, the unique nature of the
structure that we have all agreed will be best for Christchurch.
I want to once again thank the members of Parliament and the spokespe ople who
have been involved in those discussions. I would like to thank the officials for their
forbearance with us all. Politicians are very good at coming up with great ideas and then
being a little reluctant to accept that some of them might not be as good as they possibly
could be. But we were well served by officials from both the Christchurch City Council
and from Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority and the Department of the Prime
Minister and Cabinet, and I thank them for their work. I look forw ard to the Committee
stage, when I am sure they will be on hand to answer any questions that those perhaps
not quite so close to the process may have.
I do commend this bill to the House. It is a good bill, and well worth the House’s
unanimous support.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on this.
I would like to acknowledge the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, Gerry
Brownlee, who has just taken his sea t, who has taken this opportunity to come down to
the House and give a speech in the second reading. Thank you, because I think this has
been quite a unique process in that we have been able to sit down and we have been able
to thrash out what is a much -improved piece of legislation —once we have the
Supplementary Order Paper that will be tabled at the Committee stage, as the Minister
has intimated. The Minister also took the somewhat unique action of outlining Labour’s
position on this —thank you, Minister, for that —and I would like to confirm the
Minister’s statement on that. Labour is supporting this legislation, on the proviso of the
Supplementary Order Paper that the Minister has outlined in his speech being tabled. He
described those changes that will be  delivered through that Supplementary Order Paper,
which will be tabled the next time we come back into this House to debate this bill at
the Committee stage. We can offer back our support on this bill, and I am very happy
that that is the case.
The Minister talked about the need to have cross -party agreement on the issues that
relate to the recovery, the regeneration, and the governance of Canterbury around this. I
think that this is important for Cantabrians. I think that we do need to have certainty as
we enter the next phase of our history, and Cantabrians can be sure that when the
Government changes next year that there will not be major upheaval. So I thank the
Minister for thinking ahead to that, and for the work he put into that. The reason why
we wi thdrew our support after the select committee consideration was that the bill
simply was not good enough for Cantabrians. The bill did not give Cantabrians the
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9881
locally led recovery that they desired, and the locally led recovery that they deserved
and needed. I would like to thank the Minister for recognising that. I think it is a pity
that some of the Government members of the Local Government and Environment
Committee had not listened a little bit more closely at the select committee and made
that case a little earlier. But I am very grateful that the Minister did that and that we are
seeing much better legislation.
We are 5 years on from the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority legislation. I
was not a member of Parliament when the Canterbury Earthqua ke Recovery Authority
legislation was introduced into this House in the immediate aftermath of the February
quakes. I was, in fact, campaigning for the Wigram seat at the time. Those were
emergency powers for extraordinary times. I think we can all think b ack to 5 years ago
in Christchurch and what it was like. We no longer see what look like tanks in
supermarket car-parks, which is something that I think we are all very pleased to have
moved past. We no longer have the military manning a cordon around our central
business district. Sometimes it is very hard to think that it was only 5 years ago —or that
that was even 5 years ago —that we were seeing these sights on the streets of
Christchurch. And for the Labour Party, the bill that emerged, which is actually  the bill
that is sitting on the Table here today, had not moved sufficiently past this phase of our
recovery.
The bill that the majority of the select committee reported back to this House was
still too entrenched in that immediate aftermath and the emer gency powers phase of our
regeneration. We know that there is a difficult balance that needs to be struck in
Christchurch. We in the Labour Party have never advocated that now is the time to
return to business as usual —to go back and pretend that the earth quakes had never
happened and completely put everything back as if it were. The Minister alluded to the
report of the transitional board, led by Dame Jenny Shipley, and the report that it
produced made it very clear that there was an intermediate step that  was required before
that return to business as usual. And that balance did need to be struck.
We are never quiet on this side of the House when talking about the need for speed in
the Canterbury recovery. We do recognise that there do need to be some besp oke
provisions in order to have the speed that we desire in the Canterbury recovery, and that
is why we can support this bill. We also know that the Crown is making a significant
investment, and that when the Crown is making a significant investment of tax payer
money, it needs to have good oversight of that money. It needs to have responsible and
prudent oversight of that money, and I think that what we are seeing here gives the
Crown the oversight and the responsibility that it should take for taxpayer mon ey
without having to have overreaching ministerial powers that were only ever going to
serve as a roadblock to the recovery of Christchurch. So I think that we have come a
long way in terms of getting that balance right. I think one of the things that we c an see
is that the Minister has said that the Supplementary Order Paper that we have all worked
on, which he is going to table in the Committee stage —and it has actually been quite an
enjoyable process, working on that, I have to say. I have enjoyed every moment of it,
Minister, and I thank you for it.
We will strengthen the position of Regenerate Christchurch. Regenerate Christchurch
is an agency that is made up of both Crown appointments and council appointments,
and I think this reflects very well that b alance. It does preserve public input into
decisions and regeneration plans that can be made, and, as the Minister put it, it more
closely proscribes the power of the Minister, which I think is a nice way of saying that it
transitions quite a bit of power back into the hands of Cantabrians, and that is something
that I think is a positive thing. The submissions made it very clear —and there were two
very strong themes that came through from the submissions that the select committee
9882 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
heard. Local leadership wa s something that came through time and time again —80 of
the submitters focused on this as an issue that was something that needed to be given
strength.
I think that those of us from Christchurch and Canterbury can all recognise the
energy, the innovation, and the vitality that has happened in our city in the last 5 years.
For us it is in that energy, it is in that innovation, and it is in that creativity that we want
the next 5 years to lie. We think Cantabrians are going to make good decisions about
their future.
I celebrate a lot of things that are happening in our city that never would have
happened before the earthquakes. Just last weekend I spent time on an intersection in
Riccarton painting the road. We made a painted intersection in Shand Crescent. T he
idea around this, which is taken from Portland, Oregon, is about bringing communities
together and having the ability of communities to think: “Just because it’s not usually
done doesn’t mean we can’t do it.” That is the kind of spirit that has got to d efine the
next 5 years in Christchurch—people taking charge of their lives.
I would not like everyone to think I have got too carried away talking about how
much I have enjoyed this process. Of course there are questions that we still have
around provisions of this bill, and they are questions that will be fully discussed in the
Committee stage—as is appropriate —of this bill. There are questions that we need to
ask about how the agencies are going to work, and the Minister alluded to that. We are
replacing one agency, the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority, with several
agencies, some of them Crown and some of them council. How are they going to work
together? What are going to be the limits and the transparencies around those agencies?
How is it that we are going to ensure that all that is made very clear? What are the
letters of intent going to say —because the letters of intent are a very important
instrument that lies beneath this legislation, both with the Christchurch City Council and
with the Crow n entity of Ōtākaro Ltd, which is given a very large function in our
regeneration. What are that organisation’s responsibilities back in terms of reporting?
These are all discussions that we can have at the Committee stage, but I am very
happy to be able t o say that the Minister has been able to win back our support on this
bill. It was not with any pleasure that we withdrew our support at the select committee
and had to write a minority report. We voted for this bill in its first reading because we
thought that it was important that we listen to the submissions. We listened, and we are
very pleased that the Minister also listened to the very able submissions that were made
on this bill. Thank you very much.
Hon NICKY WAGNER (Associate Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery): It is my pleasure, too, to support this Greater Christchurch Regeneration
Bill. There is absolutely no doubt that we all agree that Christchurch has come a long
way since 4 September 2010. It has been a bit of an emotional rollercoaster, but we are
still learning how to reorganise our lives, how to manage our emotions, and how to cope
with grief—cope with grief for th e people whom we have lost, for the homes that have
been destroyed, and for the communities that are changed. But together we have all
survived that emergency phase. We are managing the recovery, and now it is our turn to
look forward to regeneration.
The phases all morph into each other as our lives and circumstances change and as
each of our individual futures evolve at different speeds. But 5 years on is the time to
focus on the future and embrace regeneration as the road back to business as usual: local
leadership, local management, and local control.
Regeneration is a much bigger and more exciting concept than recovery. It is about
building back better. It is about urban renewal and development, restoration,
revitalisation, and enhancement. It is our opportunity to improve the environmental, the
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9883
economic, the social, and the cultural well-being of our city and its surroundings. I think
we all know where we want to end up. I think the submitters in the Share an Idea
campaign made it very clear. We want to live in a leafy, people -friendly, vibrant city; a
place where all generations want to come to live, to work, and to play; a city that
focuses on community well-being; a city that we can be proud of; and a city that we can
all enjoy. I believe we are well on our way towards that.
I just want to make a note about the bill. The references to environmental, social, and
cultural well -being have been elevated to the purpose clause of the bill, to highlight
their importance. Many submitters thought that “regen eration” did not include
environmental well -being. Well, it does, and I am really pleased that the Local
Government and Environment Committee has recommended that it should be moved to
become more visible.
The Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill and it s Supplementary Order Paper will
provide a framework within which we can all work together to get the best possible
outcomes for our city and Greater Christchurch. The strategic partners, which are the
four councils —the Christchurch City Council, the Selwy n District Council, the
Waimakariri District Council, and Environment Canterbury —work with central
government and Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu, and we have all got roles to play to deliver
on this outcome and to prepare local organisations to take over and continue the work in
the future. This bill has only a 5 -year term, but regeneration and urban renewal will
continue well past 2021. In fact, it should be continual and ongoing, so post -2021,
Regenerate Christchurch will become a new council -controlled organisat ion. It is
crucial that we get this bill right, because it is an exciting opportunity for greater
Christchurch.
I want to thank everybody who has been involved with creating the bill: the drafters,
the submitters, the select committee, and particularly al l those members who have
worked with Minister Brownlee to make sure that this bill will support the collaborative
process that we all need to embrace as we go forward.
The bill specifically recognises local leadership, through our councils and through
Ngāi Tahu, and provides each organisation with a role in the decision making under the
Act. It requires community input to decisions into the development of regeneration
plans and the decisions on the exercise of powers under clause 42. I think the bill
represents an important milestone and allows for that much -discussed step change
move—the move from recovery to regeneration and from the Crown being in the
driver’s seat towards a progressive handover to local leaders.
Submitters were really keen that the com munity be fully included and have a strong
voice in future decisions. The Government agrees, and the bill provides many
opportunities for public input. The key is to develop a vision that will bring local people
together and allow regeneration to happen qu ickly and efficiently. Engagement in the
development of regeneration plans will be particularly important, and the bill requires
proponents at the early outline plan stage to set out the opportunities for public
engagement and how that will be undertaken. Regenerate Christchurch also has a
statutory role to engage with communities, stakeholders, and decision makers to achieve
the purpose of supporting a vibrant, thriving, and engaged Christchurch.
As I have already noted, public engagement on regeneration plans was a key issue
for submitters. I want to emphasise that the consultation provisions in this bill are a
minimum. The Government expects local leaders to identify a range of public and
stakeholder engagement opportunities for the issues covered by the  draft plan. We want
them to be creative. We want people to be excited and motivated by the possibilities for
our city.
9884 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
The St Valentine’s Day earthquake last month reminded us of just what it was like 5
years ago, but it also emphasised how far we have c ome since that time. It gave me real
confidence, seeing how our new homes and new buildings stood up so well, and any
damage—damage from rockfall, cliff crumble, or mass movement —happened only
where we expected it to happen, which was behind the barricades . There is no doubt
that Canterbury will continue to be a shaky place. We know that our geography is
constantly changing, but I think we can all be assured that our geotechnical experts have
got a really good handle on how earthquakes work in our region, a nd I think most of us
have learnt a lot about that too.
We also know that there is still more work to be done to complete the final recovery
work and before we move completely into regeneration and on to business as usual. So I
support the continuation of  the lands and works powers to finish the implementation of
the Christchurch Central Recovery Plan, and the final, very difficult, and complex
demolition that has got to be carried out on the Port Hills.
I believe the bill that is reported back from the s elect committee and its
Supplementary Order Paper will provide that step change that we all seek. It will
support a really exciting journey from recovery to regeneration, and from regeneration
to the new, local business -as-usual. Along the way, many doors will open. I think it is
really important for the inhabitants of Greater Christchurch that we can embrace the
new ideas, the new opportunities, and the new ways of working. I think that it is our
challenge and our responsibility to make really good decisio ns—good decisions for
those who have gone before us and good decisions for those who will come after us. I
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I recall when this bill was first
introduced and I suggested to the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery that he
stay in his seat —that he not stand up —because I was about to say that I supported the
bill that he had introduced. I am delighted actually that at thi s stage our support is able
to be returned. In between times, we, unfortunately, had to withdraw it because it was
clear during the select committee process that the balance had not been obtained to the
level that Labour thought was appropriate. I am also delighted that both Minister Gerry
Brownlee and, I assume, his associate, the Hon Nicky Wagner, listened to the
submitters, took a lot of time and trouble, and made an effort to engage with all other
parties in the House, to the point, I understand, that w ith the tabling of the
Supplementary Order Paper from the Minister, this bill will now receive the unanimous
support of Parliament. That is the sort of message I am delighted that Parliament will
give to Canterbury. It is not a message that we have had a l ot in the past—in the last 5½
years—and I am delighted that this is the opportunity for us to do it and that it has been
taken by the Minister.
Not much more than 5 years ago, in the February quake of 2011, events happened in
our city that really redefined Canterbury and its residents. We had the loss of thousands
of homes and 185 lives. The fact that Parliament is able to come together for the
recovery stage of that experience should be a tribute to those people who lost their lives
and to their families,  and I just want to acknowledge them. At that time, thousands of
New Zealanders rallied to support Canterbury.
I have reflected a lot —particularly around the 22 February commemorations —about
the little things that happened that meant so much to people at the time. Of course, there
were big things that happened as well, as my colleague Megan Woods said. We did
have the military everywhere. As Dr Woods would know, that was not such a bad thing
for many in our city. Many enjoyed the companionship but also the feeling of security it
gave. It was not an intimidating process at all —even the fact that we had tanks parked
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9885
in the middle of our roads, which sounds bizarre now, was reassuring for people. It gave
us comfort to know that competent professionals were there.
It was the first time in our history that every single state and the Federal Government
of Australia sent police to assist our country. That is something that we should not
forget. And, of course, the first country that sent assistance was Japan, whic h not long
after, tragically, needed assistance of its own in a much bigger event. But we had many
people in New Zealand who performed small acts of generosity that made such a big
difference to well-being.
Parliament, of course, responded in a way that we  are now considering in this
legislation, because Parliament responded with the establishment of the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Authority —CERA. We do not have women called Sarah in
Canterbury; we have CERA as an organisation. It has caused a lot of con fusion, and
could I recommend to all Ministers that they never have an organisation that can be
confused with a woman’s name, because every time we say CERA in Christchurch, we
say: “No, CERA the department, not the person.” It is a silly name, but it was not a silly
organisation; it was set up for good reasons. It gave wartime powers to the Minister, and
he needed some of them —some of them he used appropriately, as well —and some of
them he did not need to use, but they were given to him in all good faith f rom
Parliament because we thought they may have been necessary. In the end, it did not
work quite as Parliament envisaged —good things and bad things, but certainly there
were some good people.
Talking of good people, I want to pay a tribute to Michelle Mitchell, who was an
outstanding leader, not just in CERA, the organisation, but actually in the Public
Service. She tragically lost her life —a huge loss to the Public Service in Canterbury; a
huge loss to the community. She was an outstanding leader and d eserves
acknowledgment during this process.
This legislation, now, is the next step, and it is a genuine step change, which is what
we have needed for quite some time. The Minister talked about some of the iterations
that have led to this. There was the gr oup led by Dame Jenny Shipley, for whom,
members might be surprised to learn, I have a great deal of time and respect. We do not
share a single political belief, but in terms of her competence and passion she has been
outstanding, and I think she led that process towards this legislation with courage. She
is a pretty fearless person. Even the Minister would not scare her —that is right. I got
agreement there pretty swiftly.
I also want to acknowledge our three mayors, the Hon Leanne Dalziel, David Ayers,
and Kelvin Coe. They have been extraordinary contributors, not just to this process but
also to the much broader recovery in Christchurch. All three areas are at different
stages. Of course, Waimakariri and Selwyn were far more adversely affected by the
September 2010 quake than by the February 2011 quake, so they were able to get some
things started, and they are smaller areas and they had a different sort of loss. But they
have faced huge challenges, and I really admire the mayors of the three areas and the
councillors for the commitment that they have demonstrated.
I also want to acknowledge the community forum, which I understand has played a
really pivotal role in the Minister’s thinking. I regret that the Canterbury members of
Parliament did not have an y engagement with it. It was pretty well kept out of sight
from us, even though it was established under the legislation as a means of
communicating community messages to the Minister. But I have heard that the Minister
thinks highly of the work it has don e, so it certainly should be acknowledged. I know
that its chairman was recognised in the recent New Zealand Royal Honours, and that
was a good thing. I also want to acknowledge Tā Mark Solomon and Dame Margaret
9886 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
Bazley, who, again, have played a critical r ole, from their perspective and their part, in
the Canterbury recovery.
Looking specifically at the bill and where we go from here, we have had a substantial
Supplementary Order Paper signalled by the Minister and I look forward to seeing it
and hearing t he debate in the Committee stage. As I said earlier, it has acknowledged
the deficiencies that were in the bill, it has responded to the submitters’ and Canterbury
leaders’ call for a genuine transition to local leadership, and I have confidence that the
Minister’s word will be met by the detail in the Supplementary Order Paper. We will
certainly be looking at it carefully.
There are other parts of this bill that also deserve acknowledgment. One of the big
tasks that will face the bodies that are being est ablished under this legislation is
determining the future of the residential red zone. That has more significance than
disposal of land, and I want to acknowledge the way that the Waimakariri District
Council has led community discussion about this. People  did not just have a wrecked
house and leave; they had a wrecked house, and they often had lost a life within their
family—pretty well everyone in Canterbury knew somebody who died —but they were
then told that their house could not be rebuilt in the area t hat they had been living in,
and for many of them it was for many years. That loss is not able to be easily described
to people who were not part of that process. Living in a red zone became something of
a—you cannot explain it to people who were not actually there at the time.
So the process of determining what happens to that land in the future needs to
involve the people who were displaced as a result not of the quakes, but of the
Minister’s decision to zone that land red —I think quite appropriately, in  most cases—
but it needs to involve them because they have left a part of their life in that spot where
their home was. They left their neighbours and their community.
The other big part of the job that is ahead of us in Canterbury is the anchor projects.
Some of them are still hotly debated. I am not a great fan of sitting outside on a cold
winter’s night watching the Crusaders win —I would much rather sit in comfort in a
lounge. So the idea, if we are going to have a stadium, to have it covered is quite
attractive. But that sort of money as a priority —I have never been able to be persuaded
on it, particularly when I look at the significant loss that has been inflicted on Otago
because of its stadium. So we have debates about the anchor projects, but whatev er the
debate is, can we get on with some of them? There are only five out of 16, I think, that
have made any progress, and they were the big stars of the previous area.
In conclusion, one other point that I want to make is that in our community, we have
something that is outside this legislation, but I hope the Minister takes up the charge.
We want our school back on its home site in Redcliffs. It is a big part of our recovery,
even though it is not covered in the legislation, and I am sure the Minister u nderstands
that need for community schools and genuine recovery from quakes. This is the step
change that we need. I commend the Minister for his attention to the submissions and to
other parties’ concerns, and I commend this bill progressing to the next stage.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: In rising to speak in support of the
second reading of the bill, I am very conscious that I am the first non -Cantabrian to
speak in the second r eading debate. As the chairman of the Local Government and
Environment Committee, which considered this bill —which has formed a cornerstone
of a suite of legislation, in fact, relating to Canterbury, Christchurch, and the aftermath
of the earthquakes that occurred 5 years ago —I can say it has been a bit of a learning
curve and something that I have found, as I say, as a non -Cantabrian, to be a really
interesting insight into the experiences, the tragedy, the heartache, and the physical and
emotional rollercoaster that the people of Christchurch and Canterbury have undergone
since those earthquakes back in 2010.
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9887
The select committee met in Christchurch for 2½ days following the House’s rising
for the Christmas break. We travelled to Christchurch and we heard  a range of
wonderful submissions from 56 organisations and individuals, people who brought to
the select committee their experiences, their hopes for the future, and their plans for
their city and their region. We were very privileged, I think, to hear th ose submissions.
We heard them in the council chamber of Christchurch City. We heard from such a
wide range of people, from individuals through to the very big and important project
leaders and organisations that have been taking the city and the people of  Christchurch
from that phase that was initially emergency, through to recovery, and now looking
forward to the future and to regeneration, where the eyes of the city and, indeed, the
country are upon what is happening in Christchurch now and what will hap pen in the
future.
Since 2010, as a Government and as a Parliament, we have committed $16.5 billion
to the initial response, so the State has a very significant role to play in that future
direction. This bill continues the historically strong support tha t this Parliament has
provided to the people of Canterbury and Christchurch since the earthquake. Other
speakers have made reference to, and acknowledged, the very good work that has
occurred since the select committee reported back. I too want to add my e ndorsement to
that work led by the Minister the Hon Gerry Brownlee and those other members from
across the House who have individually met on a number of occasions with the Minister
to work through some of the detail and some of the difficulties that we as  a select
committee were not able to resolve before reporting back. I am delighted that as the
committee moved its report back to this Parliament, we were of a mood to say that work
still needed to be done. We knew that that needed to occur, and we knew —and hoped, I
guess—that that work would be done. I want to place on record my thanks as chairman
of the select committee to those people who have, on behalf of their city and their
region and their parties and this Parliament and the people of New Zealand, m ade that a
reality. That is a great credit to them as individuals but it is also a great credit to their
parties and to the people whom they represent.
I am not intending to go into the detail of this bill at this stage, because there will be
opportunity as we come together in the Committee of the whole House and consider the
Supplementary Order Paper, which the Minister has indicated he will be leading us
through, but the Supplementary Order Paper will include a number of changes. One will
be to ensure that there is more public input into the regeneration planning process itself.
I think that is a very good advancement. The second major point that the Supplementary
Order Paper will cover is to give Regenerate Christchurch itself a greater role in the
regeneration plans in the Christchurch district. It will also strengthen the leadership role
of Regenerate Christchurch overall, with more emphasis on public consultation around
the use of clause 42, with the Minister now required to take public submissions int o
account. I think that is a good move, as well.
I want to just, again, conclude my comments in this second reading of the bill by
thanking everybody who has been involved, thanking my colleagues on the select
committee, and thanking the officials from th e Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority and our advisers for their good work. I endorse this second reading of the bill
to the House.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: E te Māngai o Te Whare, tēnā koe; ki ngā mema e
huihui mai, tēnā koutou katoa.
[To the Deputy Speaker, greetings; to the members gathered here, greetings to you
all.]
9888 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
I am very pleased to take a call on the Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill. As Mr
Simpson said, it has been an unusual process, and I thank him and Minister Brownlee
for their comments recognising the role of other parties.
When the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act expires in April this year, with the
extraordinary powers that it provides to the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery and the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority —or CERA —it is
certainly the opportunity for a major step change in terms of who makes decisions and
how those decisions are made about Christchurch’s future. Now that we are 5 years on
from the devastating quakes in February 2011 and are over that emergency and
immediate recovery phase, we do need to see a shift from central government to local
leadership. Certai nly, the Local Government and Environment Committee did make
some good changes to the bill as introduced, one of them being the way “regeneration”
is defined. It includes, as Nicky Wagner noted, improving the environmental, economic,
social, and cultural w ell-being and resilience of communities. That is a very positive
change, particularly as the Government has stripped out from the purpose of local
government the promotion of community well -being. It is really good to see that at the
heart of this bill.
But the Green Party opposed the bill as it came back from the select committee
because it did not provide for a genuine partnership between central government and
local authorities in planning and guiding the next stage of Christchurch’s post -
earthquake future. It contained far too many hangovers from the Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery Authority era and from the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority
legislation. It left far too much power with the executive and with central government
Ministers and agencie s—particularly the Department of the Prime Minister and
Cabinet—in their ability to initiate regeneration plans and then have the relevant
Minister approve or decline those plans at the end of the process. This was particularly
important because in this bi ll it is not just the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery who can exercise these decision-making and approval powers but it is also the
relevant “Minister”, depending on the function being exercised —so that could be the
Minister of Transport, or it could be the Minister for Land Information.
That whole concentration of power at the centre was in total opposition to the strong
and eloquent call by submitters during those 2½ days of hearings in Christchurch, and
through written submissions, for local leadership, for a reduction in the power of central
government and Ministers, and for a much stronger role for people in Christchurch.
Certainly for me, it has been organisations like Greening The Rubble and Gap Filler,
with their innovative, creative, com munity-orientated projects that have been inspiring
in showing what Christchurch people are capable of. Some of the private buildings,
which are quite innovative in their design and their construction, particularly where they
use our local resource —wood—show what can happen in Christchurch when we have
local people making those decisions. It is especially important, too, when we have had
democracy denied to the Canterbury region with the half -pie, half -appointed, half -
elected model that we have got at Environment Canterbury.
This bill did need to establish a framework and a structure for decision making that
put Regenerate Christchurch as this new agency that is to symbolise and really
epitomise the partnership between central government and local government at the heart
of decision making. Regenerate Christchurch has four members on its board who are
appointed by central government, one on the nomination of Te Rūnunga o Ngāi Tahu,
and it has another three members appointed by the city council. So it is an em bodiment
of partnership. The bill as reported back did not give it a big enough role. As a result of
the negotiations with the Minister and the changes that will be in the Supplementary
Order Paper, we have got Regenerate Christchurch now having a much gre ater role in
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9889
providing advice on what plans should proceed—particularly in the residential red zone,
where Regenerate Christchurch is the only agency that can be the proponent of a
regeneration plan.
As Ruth Dyson noted, that residential red zone is a real ly central part of
Christchurch, because we are a place -based people here in Aotearoa New Zealand, and
a lot of people who had homes in the red zone still have a very strong connection with
it. As Ruth said, they left part of their lives there. The Governm ent has spent billions of
dollars in acquiring more than 6,700 homes, and there are very strong views in
Christchurch about the future of the residential red zone. We have had an 18,000 -
signature petition presented and considered by Parliament about the residential red zone.
Some have strongly promoted parks there, cycleways, community gardens —a lot of
public space. There is a need for improved flood protection, using some of that land as a
buffer from the more intense storm and weather events that we get. So the whole
planning of the residential red zone is critical to the future of Christchurch, and under
the Supplementary Order Paper, Regenerate Christchurch will be leading that.
We are very happy that there has been that quite major change there. The bil l as it
was reported back from the select committee risked emasculating Regenerate
Christchurch from the very start because it still left too much power with central
government rather than in Christchurch. So it is now giving a much more influential
role to this new agency, which has yet to be fully established but has a very effective
chair in André Lovatt, who has led some very inspiring work in restoring the
Christchurch Arts Centre. Regenerate Christchurch will be the major proponent of plans
in the res idential red zone and a major source of advice about whether regeneration
plans proceed.
One of the other areas in which we have succeeded in getting changes made is in
gaining much more transparency around the planning process —making sure that the
advice of agencies such as the other councils is made public before the public
submissions occur, and making sure, too, that the Minister has to provide clear reasons
when he or she decides whether to reject or approve a plan.
The Green Party is not totally happy  with this bill. We sought that there be a
commitment in the planning process to public hearings, because a lot of the problems
with the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority’s decision -making has been that
written submissions have been called for but t here has been no hearing process, and
there is nothing worse than faceless decision makers making quite critical decisions and
us not knowing who they are. We did not get that change in the bill, but I do encourage
Regenerate Christchurch to ensure that th ere is a public hearing process. It gives people
the opportunity to front up to decision makers and to have their say.
We remain troubled by the powers that are available to relevant Government
Ministers in clause 42, which allows them to override plans an d policies that have been
prepared through due processes under other legislation, and that means some of the
district and regional plans under the Resource Management Act, Local Government Act
planning documents and bylaws, and regional transport plans. Th e Government says
those powers will be used frugally, and the Opposition will certainly hold it to account
on that. But we did succeed here in getting some significant checks on the Minister’s
power to use clause 42, in the fact that there now must be publ ic consultation. That was
not in the bill as it was reported back, and the Minister also has to “have regard to”
public views, which is a stronger test than to just “consider” them.
This whole process has been unusual. The debate, desirably, would have hap pened at
the select committee, but we congratulate the Minister on being prepared to consider
change. I think there would have been quite considerable cost to the Government if the
bill had remained as reported back from select committee. The negotiations have been
9890 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
good in the way that they have been conducted. I thank the officials, who have put a lot
of effort into these amazing flow charts, which, when you are dealing with a plan -
making process, have been very helpful in showing the different stages and what
matters are to be considered at each stage. I would encourage the Government to use
more of this consultative process when it is developing legislation and the anchor
projects in Christchurch because we get better law where everybody is involved and
where there is a strong provision for public input. I think it shows the opportunities that
we are losing with the anchor projects and the secrecy around things like the convention
centre, which is such a critical site in the central city and is so costly. We need to have
this consultation both with the public and with other parties. But I thank the Minister for
the changes to this bill.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : I think this is going to be one of the debates and
one of the bills that I will remember most from my time in Parliament, not only because
it is such an important piece of legislation for my home city but also because of the
remarkable degree of collaboration, negotiation, and, in the end, consensus that has been
generated for the benefit of the people of Christchurch.
I want to clear up one thing at the very beginning of my speech, because in my first
