reading speech I said that New Zealand First would vote for the bill to go to the select
committee subject to a change to clause 82(3), which said: “When determining the
amount of compensation for the compulsory acquisition of land, the Minister must have
regard to the matters in subsection (4), but is not limited to determining the amount of
compensation on that basis alone and may determine whatever amount the Minister
thinks fit.” We in New Zealand First thought those words “and may determine whatever
amount the Minister thinks fit” were far too wide, and they have now been deleted, so
there is now no impediment to New Zealand First looking at the bill as a whole and
supporting it.
Consequently, we have scrutinised the bill and we have looked for a process that will
deliver our seven bottom lines. They were, firstly, to ensure the process for  initiation
would be locally led and not Crown dominated but would, of course, protect Crown
interests. Secondly, it would give the city council and Environment Canterbury the right
to be fully consulted. Thirdly, it would give plenty of opportunity for pu blic input.
Fourthly, it would not be secretive but be open and informative. Fifthly, it would seek to
enhance the environment and/or residential values of the city and/or the red zone, not
just to facilitate a sell -off of the Crown land. Sixthly, it would  ensure a much speedier
process and progress than had so far been evident but without compromising the
collaboration needed between all of the parties. Seventhly, and lastly, it would bring the
public with the parties through good communication.
I am very pleased to say that I think that the bill, as it is to be amended by the
Minister’s Supplementary Order Paper, will get very close to delivering substantially on
all seven of those bottom lines. So that means that it will be a pleasure for New Zealand
First to be able to vote in favour of the bill.
I want to say, as others have, that I am especially pleased that Minister Brownlee
brought us and other parties into the process of amending the bill through that
Supplementary Order Paper. His willingness to li sten and to change things did produce,
in the end, a consensus. I and New Zealand First appreciate the Minister’s efforts to
involve us, and we also appreciate the opportunity that we had through that process to
hear what Labour and the Greens had to say a nd also what the Mayor of Christchurch
had to say.
The Minister’s Supplementary Order Paper, to be debated more comprehensively at
the Committee stage, will mean having much more public information and opportunity
to comment and to have that input genuine ly considered and reported on. It will also
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9891
mean having a much better process for the initiation, consideration, and approval or
revocation of regeneration plans. Regenerate Christchurch is to be the primary body to
initiate, lead, review, and advise the M inister on those plans. It is a genuine partnership
because Regenerate Christchurch will have three Crown directors, three city council
ones, and one representing Ngāi Tahu.
But I would have to say that legislation can go only so far. That board must prov ide
firm leadership and must be bold in what it proposes, and must explain it well to the
people of Christchurch. It must take the people along with it. We must have faith in it,
and so must the people of Christchurch. I hope they will, given the consensus  that has
been possible so far.
Without trying to pre-empt the Committee stage, I want to mention some of the most
important provisions and changes that have been agreed to and that led to New Zealand
First supporting the bill as it will be amended. One i s clause 12A(1) and new clause
12A(3)(c). Those are important changes because only Regenerate Christchurch can now
be a proponent for the red zone plans and may be a proponent for the Christchurch
district plans, as, of course, the other strategic partners  may be, as well, including
Environment Canterbury and Ngāi Tahu.
New clause 13A(2) ensures that statements to the Minister on the views of other
parties on an outline plan must now be made public on the internet, and there are also
similar requirements in new clause 20A concerning the views of parties to an approval
of a draft plan. It is very important that the public be properly advised in that way.
Clause 18(2) requires the Minister, in approving or declining an outline plan, to
“have particular regard” to the views of Regenerate Christchurch and the other partners.
Those words are repeated elsewhere for approvals of final plans and for revocations.
Those are very important words in order to limit the executive power of the Minister
and preserve the cred ibility and leadership functions of, especially, Regenerate
Christchurch and also, of course, the two councils that will be involved as far as
Christchurch City is concerned.
New clauses 22A and 22H set out the process for outline plans for Christchurch Ci ty
district and for the red zone. They include the need for a clear statement of intentions
and scope, time frames, opportunities for public engagement, how the costs are to be
met—a very important consideration —and that a proponent must seek the views of its
partners. Regenerate Christchurch must get the consent of Ōtākaro Ltd as the
landowner, but Ōtākaro Ltd cannot refuse “except for reasons that are consistent with
the purposes of the Act.” So there is, I think, an appropriate balance between all of the
objectives that are required.
I also want to mention new clause 20(2)(j), which sets out the requirements
prerequisite to ministerial approval. I think this is a very important new provision. There
must be a recommendation by Regenerate Christchurch for a plan for Christchurch
District, and that must contain advice, a statement of the views of the other partners, and
also advice on how such views have been considered and addressed. There are similar
requirements elsewhere for approvals and amendments and,  of course, for revocations,
which include a requirement for Regenerate Christchurch to review and make
recommendations to the Minister. So, effectively, it is going to be Regenerate
Christchurch that leads and advises, and it will not, effectively —in my v iew—be the
Minister who really makes the decision. His function, I think, is going to be relatively
formal. The grounds upon which he could refuse would be very limited.
There is a lot more in the bill —many other changes. But one of the most important
ones in the bill is clause 97, which specifies the roles of the city council and the
Minister to oversee and manage the interests of both in Regenerate Christchurch. That
means there will have to be joint responsibility and commitment of resources, as there
9892 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
should be. In clause 97A there may be a letter of expectations along those lines, and I
hope that there will be, because that is a very good way of setting out how that joint
responsibility will be met.
Finally, it is a pleasure to see a consensus on what is going to be a very good bill and
a very important bill for the future of Christchurch City and its people. I think it will
ensure a robust process, focusing on regeneration rather than just recovery, that properly
balances speedy redevelopment —which is much in need —with the wider public
interest, especially for an excellent environment and for the hoped -for public recreation
facilities. It is going to be a pleasure to support the bill.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to take a
short call in support of the Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill. My colleague Mr
Scott Simpson acknowledged that he is not a Cantabrian. I too am not a Cantabrian; I
am a Southl ander. So, therefore, I think it is appropriate to acknowledge that
Cantabrians are still very much on the minds of Southlanders. Our sympathies went out
to Cantabrians, with the horror that they experienced 5-odd years ago.
There is still very much an acknowledgment of what Cantabrians have had to endure
and of their strength of character in surviving and living in Christchurch while the
recovery has been going on and the city is being rebuilt. There certainly is a strength of
character that Cantabrians exude, and we acknowledge them for their persistence. But it
is certainly a relief now, after one of the most ambitious rebuild projects that we have
undertaken in New Zealand, to be moving forward into a regeneration phase. I am sure
it is very much a relief for Cantabrians.
This bill —as I understand it, having not sat on the Local Government and
Environment Committee—is a very good one that, through collaboration, will establish
Regenerate Christchurch, which is a jointly controlled Crown organisation, with the
Christchurch City Council. It will lead the charge in respect of regeneration in the
Greater Christchurch region. I think one of the best parts of the bill is that it is returning
to a local leadership model, in that —well, where else should owners hip of the design
and the planning and the moving forward of Christchurch rest but with Cantabrians
themselves?
I think this is a great win for Cantabrians as they look to the future, as they look to
rebuilding a very positive, modern city that will serve  them well into the future. I wish
them all the very best with that. I look forward to the results.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Mojo Mathers—a 5-minute call.

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on the Greater
Christchurch Regeneration Bill. You know, it has been 5 long years since the
Christchurch earthquakes, and the city is still very much, in many areas, in a bit of a
limbo. It feels like time is going past, and it is going to be fantastic to actually see the
rebuild and things moving forward.
I want to acknowledge the hard work of my colleague Eugenie Sage and other MPs
who have helped to make this bill a better bill with the Supplementary Orde r Paper
coming up, and who have pushed really hard for local leadership, and for Regenerate
Christchurch to be at the heart of decision making and to have a much greater role in the
development and planning of the anchor projects and the residential red zo ne areas, and
so on. It is incredibly important that that does happen, and it is a relief to be at this point
where there has been sufficient accommodation made for these very important issues
that have been raised, so that we can now support the bill.
What I want to focus on —rather than rehashing what everyone else has said before
me—is the importance of all these plans for the city incorporating genuine accessibility
and universal design principles into the planning, the design, and the implementation.
This is what the people of Christchurch want. It was one of the most popular ideas and
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9893
common themes that was put forward during the Share an Idea campaign several years
ago, and it is absolutely critical to social recovery. We have a golden opportunity righ t
now to rebuild Christchurch as the most accessible city in the world. There are
absolutely no barriers to stop that from happening, given political will, local leadership,
and a genuine commitment to making that happen. It would be a city that is accessi ble
for all—for children, for the elderly, for parents, for the disabled —and it is critical to
the social recovery. I have constantly raised this issue —will the city be accessible, and
will there be a commitment to accessibility implemented and taken on bo ard by the
planners and designers at all stages —and repeated assurances have been given to me
that all the anchor projects would be accessible and that there would be independent
accessibility audits incorporated into every step, from design through to
implementation.
Now we have seen that some anchor projects have been accessible, such as the Bus
Interchange, which is a very good example of that, where all sorts of features have been
incorporated to make using the Bus Interchange a generally positive and inclusive
experience for many users. But there are other areas where they have not got it right,
and probably the most striking example of that recently was the Margaret Mahy Family
Playground. This was a playground that was welcome. People were so excited  when it
opened. There was just this massive positive vibe and people were going to it, and then
a few days later there were people saying: “Well, actually, my child can’t use it. It’s not
accessible for children in a wheelchair. There are not enough facil ities for people in
wheelchairs to use it.”
This was an appalling failure and breakdown of the planning process. It was a
reversal of what we really want and what we mean by an accessible city. We must not
exclude children from that conceptualisation and we must not exclude disabled people.
It must be independently audited because you cannot rely on the various design groups
having in-house expertise. These projects, right from the start, must be independently
audited. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Poto Williams—5 minutes.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: I must admit that when I
reviewed my notes for my first reading speech on this bill, I was less generous than I am
going to be in this contribution. Before the bill had gone through the process that we
have heard talked about in this House this afternoon, I had some concerns about
whether it w as fit for purpose for the people of the area that I represent. My concerns
were about the Minister’s powers, particularly those to acquire and dispose of land at
whatever price he could determine. I was also concerned that the public were by and
large exc luded from many of the discussions on the facilities and the future use of
particular areas in which they would have a significant interest.
But I have to say that the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery has listened
to the people of Canterbury and  has engaged in a process that has garnered widespread
support across the House. It is not entirely perfect, but it has gone a long way to
ensuring that the interests of the people of Canterbury have been reflected in the
legislation and, more important, in the Supplementary Order Paper that will come to this
House during the Committee stage.
I really want to focus my contribution on what this means for the people of
Christchurch East. I have to say that during the passage of the last few years the people
of the electorate of Christchurch East have been very vocal about what they would like
to see within the residential red zone, which sits largely within the boundaries of the
Christchurch East electorate. There have been processes and opportunities for the
community to engage with, and I want to mention one in particular, which happened 18
months ago, and that is the EVO::SPACE project. That was an IT -driven consultation
9894 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
process for people to actually tell us —those who would be making decisions about the
future of their particular area—what they would like to see done with the residential red
zone, an extensive area that actually covers some of the most beautiful parts of
Christchurch, particularly with the Avon River flowing through it.
There were some fanta stic ideas from treetop cafes and ideas from the Eden Project
through to camellia and rhododendron groves, and on to things like Barkerton Park —a
place to go and let your dog run free. That process was about giving the people of the
area—who actually have a vested interest, whether they continue to live there or
whether they have had to leave the area and leave behind a significant part of their
emotional attachment to the area —an opportunity to feel like they could contribute to
the future of that particular area.
When we are considering plans for the use of the residential red zone, I would ask
that our ability to communicate well with the community and give it an opportunity to
have input into that process is significant, because it was not, as the Hon Ru th Dyson
has expressed it, just about the loss of land. There were people who lived there. There
were families who grew there. On some of the properties there were heritage trees that
had been there for over 125 years. There were people who have significan t history
attached to the area. So these people have a vested interest in ensuring that their views
and their hearts and souls go into any future development.
I just want to finish my contribution by saying that I agree with Mojo Mathers that
there have be en opportunities missed here —particularly around accessibility —but also
around ensuring that facilities are not taken out of the area before replacements can be
put in. Here I want to talk particularly about the Burwood Birthing Unit, which has been
lost t o the east of Christchurch because of what happened on Valentine’s Day only a
few weeks ago —the 5.7 quake —and, also, the Central New Brighton School pool,
which is a huge loss to our community as we do not have a pool in the area.
I do want to say that th is has been a very positive process and, along with my
colleagues, I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I stand to take a short call on the Greater
Christchurch Regeneration Bill in the name of the Hon Gerry Brownlee. I am very
pleased to do this because we are starting to move down the road a bit on this bill, and it
is a bill moving from recovery to regeneration—regeneration focusing on urban renewal
and development, and on resto ration and enhancement of the city facilities. These are
really important because this Government has been working very hard at restoring the
various facilities that the city lost in the 2011 earthquake. Some of those facilities are
sporting facilities. Th e Hagley Oval was opened last year and was able to host the
Cricket World Cup. It is a beautiful facility. I have been there a few times, enjoying a
few meetings there. The next one is the Bus Interchange, which had a little bit of a spit
and a fart there along the way when it first opened and there was a little bit of
congestion there with a few little trips. But after everything is said and done, people got
used to it and it is pumping along very nicely.
Then the last facility in 2015 that we opened was the Margaret Mahy Family
Playground. That is an amazing playground. I was visiting there just recently and was
really impressed with the layout that that has for not only the people of Christchurch but
also the people who are visiting, because we need thes e facilities to bring in the tourists
and bring in the overseas travellers, so they too can bring their money into Christchurch
and spend it to help us with the regeneration as well. In addition to all of these
achievements in 2015 there has also been the increased funding to the Metro Sports
Facility, as well as the public sector precinct construction that has been happening. That
is billions and billions of dollars’ worth that has gone into the city thus far.
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9895
I want to take the opportunity to thank the w orkers of the Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery Authority. They were the ones who started the recovery process. They have
done a wonderful job to date, and as they slowly move out —because they have done
their bit; we are morphing into Regenerate Christchurch with a whole new team of
people—maybe some of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority people may
just go in there because it is quite good to have some old heads in there along with some
new heads. We have started working, also, towards having a gover nance structure. As
the Minister has said, we have opened it up and we have seen that bureaucracy does rule
and reign within the city as well.
In some of the final parts of my contribution I do want to talk a little bit about the flat
areas of the red zone, which the previous speaker, Poto Williams, just touched a little bit
on. I also want to acknowledge those volunteers who have been caring for the red zone
flat areas through donations from the public or from their own personal pockets. I look
forward to where we are going to be going with the red zone areas. There is a lot of
work and a lot of thinking that needs to go on around there.
Finally, the Stronger Christchurch Infrastructure Rebuild Team, otherwise known as
SCIRT, is now over in the eastern pa rts of Christchurch. It is going along very well.
Yes, businesses in Parklands and Bower Avenue are feeling the pinch with some of the
missed opportunities, but by the time the Stronger Christchurch Infrastructure Rebuild
Team has finished, which is by the  end of this year, that area of Parklands and Bower
Avenue will look absolutely amazing with its new horizontal infrastructure that is going
on at the moment. It does hurt. It does hurt, but I can see that some of the businesses
have been quite innovative.  They have been meeting with Stronger Christchurch
Infrastructure Rebuild Team and Downer Group, and the electorate MP, Poto Williams,
and I have been attending these meetings. It is quite good to get around the table and to
actually nut out and help to fi nd some ways that businesses can keep flourishing, albeit
at a slower pace, while these repairs are going on.
All in all, this is a very good bill. I look forward to it passing into legislation with the
amendments in the Supplementary Order Papers that th e Minister has done. I think it is
good, not just for the people of this House but for all New Zealand, when we can see
that the whole of Parliament is working for the well -being of all New Zealanders. I
commend the bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I join, as a member of Parliament in
Canterbury, with other colleagues in welcoming the passage of the Greater Christchurch
Regeneration Bill. I think it is in teresting, though, to recast a little history. I commend
Minister Brownlee. I know that Minister Brownlee and my good self have often had a
colourful and wide -ranging relationship, and occasionally we have crossed swords —in
the best of humour, I know.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Tell us more.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Tell you more —I could. I could go on for hours,
but I am sure the Assistant Speaker would fall asleep with some of my anecdotes.
However, I will say that that Minister Brownlee,  to use the Thatcherite expression, is
not one for turning, and over many years he has not been a person who has been willing
to change his mind on various things. But I do commend him—
Denis O’Rourke: He had an epiphany.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: An epiphany, yes. Maybe —being a good Catholic,
like me—he had a road to Damascus moment. But I do commend him on this occasion.
I do note that there were members in the Local Government and Environment
Committee—some of whom have spoken—who actually opposed the changes that were
put forward by Megan Woods and others, and I have to commend Minister Brownlee as
the person who stepped in and said: “No, no, we’re going to listen and we’re going to
9896 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016
make those changes.” It is difficult  in politics to say: “Well, there may be somebody
with a better idea or a better way to do things.” None of us have a monopoly on
knowledge in these instances, and Minister Brownlee has indeed recognised —after 5
years, but he has none the less recognised —that we have really smart people in
Canterbury. We have always had incredibly entrepreneurial people, people who have
demonstrated—not just talked about it but demonstrated —the wealth of knowledge and
commitment that they have to our province and have alway s been willing, from day
one, if they were allowed to do it, over the last 5 years to step up and say: “We’re
prepared to have to have a go and work our guts out to get our province and our city
back off its knees.” I would point out, just for the record, that they have not really had
that opportunity, in a great way, over the last 5 years.
However, let us be positive about this new world order. This bill, I think —if
implemented correctly—will allow the unleashing of that energy and allow those smart
folks in Canterbury to lead that recovery from grassroots, to have a locally led recovery,
and to have local and substantial input that is not just dealt with via lip service but
actually makes a massive and real and high -quality contribution to the recovery of  our
province. That is something that has been a huge chasm, a huge gap, over the last 5
years.
People have talked about the Margaret Mahy Family Playground. People in this
House have talked about the Metro Sports Facility, an anchor project that we do not
have. People have not talked about, for instance, the great need —and we have got a
couple of tourism experts over there —for a convention centre in Christchurch. We
desperately need that as an anchor project because we know there is hundreds of
millions of dollars’ worth of capital sitting there —it will not sit there for ever —waiting
to be unleashed in respect of infrastructure and hotels. We know, of course, that one of
our biggest supermarket chains wants to put a massive supermarket, I am told, right in
the centre of Christchurch, but it needs to know where the centres of population will be,
where the business activity will be, whether there will be a stadium, whether there will
be a convention centre, and whether these promises will come to pass so that the private
sector—which is far better at these projects than, I would wager, any bureaucrat or
politician is—can unleash that capital and build its businesses and bring life back into
the centre of our city.
So I welcome the bill, and I say to my St Bede ’s College counterpart, Mr Brownlee,
in all seriousness, that I am gratified and grateful that he has been prepared to listen to
alternative points of view; that he has been prepared to say “OK, we’re going to gut this
bill, and we’re going to insert these  changes.”, which ourselves and the Christchurch
City Council and others proposed; and that he listened to submission after submission
from people who said: “Look, we want to lead our recovery as a city, as a province. We
want to lead it as local people. W e want to take responsibility —greater and greater and
responsibility.”
Those local people are actually the experts, because they live there, and they have
lived through tragedy, they have lived through adversity, and many continue to do that.
They have battled every day, many of them, to survive and to look after their families in
pretty strenuous social and economic circumstances. They have lived it. I said, when I
had the spokesperson role, when the earthquake actually struck, that I hoped we did not
get an army —no disrespect —of Wellington bureaucrats parachuting in with their
clipboards and their penholders, saying: “Tut, tut, tut!” and “We have all the answers.”
Sadly, I would argue that we have done exactly that over the last 5 years. And it does
surprise me that many of the folks on the other side who purport to be great free -
marketers—those who just want to let the juices flow, as it were, whether that be in a
business sense or economically or socially—allowed that to happen.
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9897
Kiwis are smart. Kiwis in  Canterbury are smart. People who have empathy are those
who lived it, breathed it, ate it, dealt with it, and survived through it every day for 5
years; who live with it today; and who lived with it on Valentine’s Day, when we had
the big shove. We have t hem every couple of days, and people get scared —and there
are people in our province who are genuinely scared. There are massive mental health
issues, and I hope that —because we in politics, especially on this side, get accused of
being political every tim e we raise issues. It is a nice little cheap shot by some, which
actually labels and negates any of the positive input. We know in mental health that kids
and adults are struggling every day. We know our district health board is under massive
strain. For those who thought that in any conventional sort of disaster you throw a few
dollars at mental health for a couple of years, Christmas comes along, in summer the
sun is shining, and everybody is happy again, they have not picked off the case studies
around the world of natural disasters and they have not listened to clinicians and experts
who tell you quite clearly that it will be 10, 15, or possibly 20 years before some of
these folks work these problems through in medical terms to get it out of their system s,
or, if they cannot, they learn to cope in their own way. To do that, they need assistance
and they need mental health resources, and I implore the Government—using this bill as
an opportunity to do so—to address those issues.
If anybody thinks they hav e gone away, go and talk to your local high school,
primary school, or intermediate school principal and ask what is happening to many
kids in our community. If anybody thinks those mental health issues have gone away,
make sure you are in town the next ti me we have a good shove, like we did on
Valentine’s Day, and wander around and talk to people, many of whom —I could use
some vernacular, but I will not —are scared, very scared. It just brings that nightmare
back, again and again. This is not the fault of p oliticians; this is the fault of mother
Nature. But, none the less, it exists, and none the less it is real. So I hope, out of this
bill, that local folks have a greater say and have greater standing with the Government
and with the Minister—whomever he or she may be—and Ministers involved within the
intertwined portfolios that will deal with the earthquake situation going forward. I hope
that those people—those respected community leaders—are listened to.
I had a meeting with the Canterbury Employers’ Cha mber of Commerce, along with
other colleagues, and even Peter Townsend, the chief executive of the chamber of
commerce, said to us very clearly some weeks ago that he was deeply concerned —
deeply concerned—about the mental health issues and the lack of reso urces. I hope—he
may not feel he can say those things publicly—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: You can say it for him.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Yes, well, I have helped him out with that. I hope,
given that he has standing —and he is a  respected senior business person, a highly
respected person in our community, and I know he has standing with the National Party
and with the Government, as a senior business leader —that those members listen to
Pete Townsend, as he, I am sure, will make r epresentations, if he has not already, as a
responsible community leader in Canterbury on those issues.
I commend the bill. I think it is one of those rare moments in a Parliament where
Opposition members were allowed to put up counter ideas and were not napalmed by a
Government through political labels —where a Government and a Minister respected
those ideas and listened —and I think we have a better piece of legislation. I think the
people of Canterbury will say: “Hey, those politicians in Wellington actua lly, now and
again, do listen to us.” I look forward to those wonderful, smart community leaders
within my province getting to take some of the reins back, getting to take some of the
power back, and getting to put their fantastic skill base to work as we move through
serving our community in this recovery.
9898 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 17 Mar 2016

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Kia ora, e Te Mana Whakawā. It is indeed my honour
to be the last speaker in the Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill’s second  reading. It
is also my honour as mana whenua, from a whānau that comes from that region that can
date back over seven generations. One thing that Ngāi Tahu have always said is that it is
very important to actually look back to know where you are going to move forward.
What I want to do is just quote a speech from our Governor -General on the first
anniversary for the 185 victims of the Christchurch earthquake because, in a lot of ways,
what Sir Jerry Mateparae said is coming to fruition with this bill. So,  just to quote him,
on the first anniversary he said that while it was a time for reflection, the 1 -year
anniversary marked “the start of a new day and a new beginning for all of us, and
especially the people of Christchurch and Canterbury.” He said that “ a new and vibrant
city can arise.” in the future, although “Achieving that aspiration will take time.” He
said: “Lives, communities and cities are not built in a day.” It would be achieved, he
said, because of the resilience and preparedness Cantabrians ha d demonstrated over the
previous year. He said: “It will be achieved because the people of Christchurch and
Canterbury do not walk that pathway alone. Your extended family —the New Zealand
family—are walking alongside you. … For your tragedy has been New Ze aland’s
tragedy. Such are the ties of this nation that there are few among us who have been
untouched by what occurred.”
We have heard today in this second reading a lot of what has happened, particularly
around the emergency and the incredible things that  went on, particularly following the
aftermath. The thing is that he talked about resilience; he talked about vibrancy. When
you look at the stages of the Christchurch earthquake, you had the emergency, then
there was the recovery, and then there is what w e now call the rebuild and the transition
from that rebuild into regeneration. This is what this bill is about.
One thing that came out of that speech, I think, which was also talked about by other
speakers on that day, was that there also needed to be re ally good leadership to be able
to achieve what was identified on that day. What we have in the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery, the Hon Gerry Brownlee, is exactly that leadership —that
leadership over the last 5 years. When we talk about the Ca nterbury Earthquake
Recovery Authority, when we talk about the Stronger Christchurch Infrastructure
Rebuild Team, and when we talk about the Christchurch Central Development Unit, we
cannot forget these people, either, who worked within that because they a ctually gave
their hearts and souls to be able to contribute through all of those phases, particularly
around the recovery and the rebuild. Just think, now that there is a transitional process
going on at the moment, what they must be thinking, around: “Am  I going to have a
job? Am I going to continue through into this next phase?”. I think it is important that
we think about them, as well.
But coming to the bill, it is really great to hear from the other side of the House. The
previous speaker, the Hon Cl ayton Cosgrove—if Labour was in Government he would
be sitting in Mr Brownlee’s seat, I am sure, and he would have been doing the same
thing. I cannot see anything different. Is it not great to see that we do have that sort of
cross-party, bipartisan thing  that we call kotahitaka? What we have is that the major
stakeholders have all come together. There are the councils, the businesses, and also the
iwi, as well. We have mentioned the iwi here. This is the great thing about being on the
Local Government and Environment Committee, because we are able to strengthen the
input of the iwi. So that is really—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Why did you oppose it? Why did you oppose the measures
that the Minister—

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: I cannot see him, so I will not answer. I think the important
thing—to keep moving on this —is the fact that nothing was opposed, because what we
17 Mar 2016 Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill 9899
have in the end is that everyone is hoe-ing the waka together. Everyone is moving in the
same direction.
At the end of the day this bill is a great bill, even if some on the other side do not like
it. This is a great bill —it is together. This Minister is the Minister who made it happen.
He would be damned if he did or damned if he did not, but at the end of the d ay we are
the Government that is leading this through and we are actually taking it by the horns
and really moving it and developing, and Christchurch will be one of the greatest and
newest cities in the world. It is all to do with this side of the House, or a lot of it, but at
least we have got some real working togetherness here at the moment, even if what we
hear on the other side is negative, because to those members the glass is always half
empty—it is always half empty. Here it is half full. So, kia o ra. I commend this bill and
I look forward to working with the other side of the House on the regeneration of
Christchurch. That is what it is about.
Amendments recommended by the Local Government and Environment Committee
by majority agreed to.
Bill read a second time.
GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS (WINE AND SPIRITS) REGISTRATION
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.role: Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
items.text: I
move, That the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment
Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Primary Production Committee to consider
the bill. This bill amends the Geograph ical Indications (Wines and Spirits) Registration
Act 2006. A geographical indication is a name —usually a regional name —that is used
to identify the origin of goods where a quality reputation or other characteristic of the
goods is related in some essentia l way to their geographical origin. Foreign wine and
spirit producers use geographical indications to identify their products. Well -known
examples of these are champagne and Scotch whisky.
In New Zealand the main user of geographical indications is the loc al wine industry.
Geographical indications used in New Zealand wines include such terms as
Marlborough, Martinborough, and Gimblett Gravels. Over time, as an area’s reputation
grows, the name adds value. New Zealand wines already attract a premium in forei gn
markets, and we want to preserve that and build on it.
It is worth taking a moment to reflect on the amazing progress that the New Zealand
wine industry has had in the last decade or so. It was only in the late 1990s that the New
Zealand wine exports br oke the $100 million barrier. It is now worth $1.5 billion in
exports in the last year, and rising fast. That is part of the diverse export economy that
sustains our living standards here in New Zealand. The Trans -Pacific Partnership, with
its promise of i mproved market access, is a boost to this industry, and we have heard a
lot about that over the last few weeks. This bill will also help.
If I can go and give a bit of background, the World Trade Organization Agreement
on Trade -related Aspects of Intellect ual Property Rights —otherwise known as the
TRIPS agreement —obliges New Zealand to provide protection for geographical
indications for wines and spirits. Geographical indications are currently protected in
New Zealand by a range of measures, including the t ort of passing off, the Fair Trading
Act 1986, the Trade Marks Act 2002, and the relevant provisions of the Australia New
Zealand Food Standards Code.
The Geographical Indications (Wines and Spirits) Registration Act 2006 provides for
a registration system of geographical indications, but this Act is not yet in force. It was
9900 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
passed in anticipation that New Zealand would soon begin negotiations on a wine
agreement with the European Union. However, negotiations never began. At the time
the local wine industry  did not have an interest in registering geographical indications,
so the Act was never brought into force.
More recently, however, the local wine industry has become concerned about the
potential misuse of New Zealand geographical indications in export ma rkets. This
misuse has the potential to adversely affect the reputation of New Zealand wine, which,
as I have said, commands a premium price in export markets. The further the premium
grows, the further the potential for misuse increases. The risk can be m itigated by
registering New Zealand geographical indications in these export markets. However,
most countries will not register geographical indications unless they are registered in
their country of origin. As a result, the Government has decided to bring  this Act into
force. An additional advantage of bringing the Act into force is that it will support New
Zealand’s interest in launching free-trade agreement negotiations between New Zealand
and the European Union.
Before the Act can be brought into force,  some amendments are necessary to clarify
provisions in the Act and to ensure that the registration process runs smoothly and
sustainably. These amendments are contained in the amendment bill. Most of these
amendments are minor and technical. Some amendments are more significant; I will just
quickly mention these.
The geographical indication registration expires after 10 years unless a renewal fee is
paid. The renewal fees will contribute towards the ongoing maintenance of the register
of geographical indications and help to keep the initial application fees down.
The second one is that we provide that the terms “New Zealand”, “South Island”, and
“North Island” will be protected as registered geographical indications without the need
for an application to be made. These terms are used as geographical indications by local
wine producers, but might not otherwise meet the definition of “geographical
indication” in the Act.
The Registrar of Geographical Indications would be given the power to refuse to
register a geographical indication if registration or use of the indication would be likely
to be offensive to a significant section of society, including Māori. This mirrors the
provision in the Trade Marks Act and ensures that the geographical indications that
might be refused registration as trademarks on offensiveness grounds cannot be
registered as geographical indications.
Once the amendment bill is enacted, the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits)
Registration Act can then be brought into force, and it  will be possible for interested
parties to apply to register geographical indications. The Act will be administered by the
Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand, which is also responsible for other
registered intellectual property rights such as trademarks and patents.
This is, I think, an important step in the development and maturity of the New
Zealand wine industry. I hope that it will provide an opportunity to help sustain the
progress that we are making in this important area of the New  Zealand economy, and it
is, of course, an important provider of much joy and merriment and happiness to New
Zealanders and people around the world who enjoy the New Zealand wine in its great
variety and wonderful, wonderful quality. I do move that this bi ll now be referred to the
Primary Production Committee for consideration. Thank you.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: It is a genuine pleasure to speak to the
Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Re gistration Amendment Bill at its first
reading, and, for the benefit of the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, I will

17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9901

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: The more you drink, the better it gets.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Well, that is your opinion. This piece of legislation is needed to
protect and also to increase the potential earnings for New Zealand, whether it be from
Central Otago—and I will come to a story around that, of a recent example, soon —the
Canterbury region, the Wairarapa, the Hawke’s Bay, or Waiheke Island. Our wine is so
good that there could be a certain element within the industry that may want to take a
geographic indication and pass its product off as one of the quality products that we
produce here in New Zealand.
The recent event that I was talking about was that I was enjoying dinner with a
parliamentary delegation for the Government Administration Co mmittee in Canberra.
We were talking to the President of the Senate, Stephen Parry, at a dinner that he
hosted, and I had the pleasure of sitting at the table with a former Speaker of the
Australian Parliament, Bronwyn Bishop. The President of the Senate w as talking about
how good the quality of Tasmanian wine was, and one of our delegates said: “But have
you tasted some of our Central Otago Pinots, though, Mr President?”. Bronwyn Bishop,
who is no longer the Speaker of Parliament House, said: “Oh no, they’ re rubbish.” She
almost caused a diplomatic incident there, and we did commit to sending her a bottle of
good Central Otago Pinot to prove just how good our wine is. But she has got problems
about helicopters and her own transport, so I do not think she is  hanging out for that
bottle of wine.
This piece of legislation will ensure precision around where wine comes from. I note
that the Minister did go into some detail about the functions of this piece of legislation,
but I think one of the most important one s—certainly the most important one that the
officials are pushing in the regulatory impact statements —is that in the past, you could
pass off New Zealand wine as being wine from a region if 85 percent of the grapes in
the bottle of wine were from that regi on. We have gone from a situation where you
could have 85 percent —and let us choose a region at random; say, the Hawke’s Bay —
of the grapes from the Hawke’s Bay, and 15 percent of the grapes in that make -up of
wine could be from anywhere else, including overseas.
To make sure that there is certainty and integrity in our product, this piece of
legislation says that that is not good enough to be labelled as being from a particular
region in New Zealand, or from New Zealand, and we are going to make sure that t hey
are 100 percent from that region or from New Zealand. I think that, as an exporter of
wine, our country needs that certainty in other trade markets so that for people buying
our wine—and I know that it is going great guns in the UK —they have certainty that it
is not a blend of our grapes and Australian grapes, but it is a 100 percent New Zealand
product.
9902 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
I think that precision of information will ensure the integrity of our exports overseas,
and I understand that, also, it is a reciprocal agreement with  deals that we are looking to
do, especially with the EU, in that because they want certainty about the product that we
send to them, we will have certainty about the product that they send to us. It is not so
much wine coming across that I think we would want certainty with. I am a whisky
drinker, so I want to know with a decent amount of certainty that the whisky that I buy
of a particular brand and from a particular place does come from that particular place. I
think it is even -stevens to make sure that if we have certainty from our end as a
consumer, they have certainty about the product that we are sending away as well.
The Minister also made out the case for registration, in that it lasts for 10 years. One
issue that I think we will want some certainty  and some clarity around in the select
committee is how the registration system will work, and to make sure —and I am sure
that the wine industry will make a submission —that the system around payment and
costs for running the registration system is fair and  that it is not too onerous, especially
front-loading it when you register a geographic indication the first time. It gives them
the ability to spread it over time to make sure we are not putting a massive burden on
winegrowers and wine producers at the ve ry beginning, which would make it very
difficult for them to, I guess, at the first instance, make sense of that.
Going back to some of the indications, from my reading of some of the publications
that came out when former Minister of Trade Tim Groser said  that this piece of
legislation would be introduced to the House, they said that it would also prevent the
use of indications such as “in the style of”. You will not be able to say “in the style of
Marlborough” or “in the style of New Zealand” or “in the s tyle of Hawke’s Bay”
because, I guess, some producers could try to use that sneaky language to get out of
that.
I think that is tricky and sneaky, and I think we have seen an example of that
recently, with “in the style of Eminem”, “in the style of Coldpla y”—the taking of
someone else’s intellectual property and using it for your own benefit and calling it
“pretty legal”. In this instance, it will not be “pretty legal”; it will be illegal. To say that
things are “in the style of Marlborough” or “in the style of Hawke’s Bay” will no longer
be allowed. Maybe we could transfer that over to other areas and say, well, “in the style
of Eminem” and “in the style of Coldplay” is not really fair, either. So let us see
whether we can get some agreement there as well.
That aside, there is massive potential here for our wine industry to use this as a
selling point. I think there have been indications from those in the industry themselves
that if we do not take this action with this piece of legislation, there will be ris ks to our
reputation and risks to our brand, and it will prevent them from telling a story about
wine that comes from their specific region, or wine that has come from our country.
Having a look at some of the media that came out when this piece of legisla tion was
first mooted, Blair Walter from Felton Road Wines was talking about his particular
brand of Riesling. Again, I think the Minister said that this was updating a piece of
legislation that was passed in 2006. It has not been enacted yet, so we are up dating it to
make it more modern. Mr Walter said that the rules were made years ago to protect the
consumer, to ensure that what they were getting was a good quality wine, and he is
right. But he said that nowadays as that wine producer, it is almost becom ing a trade
barrier if we cannot guarantee that a wine is from a particular area. So I guess it makes
this piece of legislation necessary, to protect not only the brands and the consumers of
New Zealand but also the potential trade earnings we can get from  really, really good
wine that, as I said at the beginning of my speech, is heading overseas. I understand it
was somewhere in the vicinity of $1.4 billion of exports for New Zealand wine to the
year to September last year. That is a lot of money —and there is a lot more, potentially,
17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9903
that we can earn—and there is nothing to protect those potential earnings. This piece of
legislation should be supported.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: I would like to start by acknowledging
the knowledge of the previous speaker, Kris Faafoi, of the subject, but I would like to
make one small correction: 85 percent of the grapes that go into making up a wine can
indeed come from one geographical indicator, and 15 percent of the remaining, if the
grower chooses to, must come from within New Zealand. So that still remains, but it has
been changed to make it clear that the grapes cannot come from overseas if a grower
wants to claim that same geographical indicator.
I want to bring a little bit of my own personal experience to this debate. I was
involved with New Zealand Winegrowers prior to the Geographical Indications (Wine
and Spirits) Registration Act being passed in 2006. We sought to have that bill passed,
and then we sought to have it not enacted, really for good reasons around trade. Trade
with the EU can be fraught —particularly around agricultural products —and the one
card that we had to play was not having the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits)
Registration Act enforced in law at that stage.
However, time has moved on. We are now in a position where we want that to pass
through, and the wine industry wants that. I am no longer involved in it, but I do note
that New Zealand winegrowers are present h ere today. It is a very important bill. The
New Zealand wine industry relies on selling on its good name, and I think one of things
to bring to this debate is how the geographical indication really is so important in selling
wine. The consumers like to know the provenance of the product that they are drinking.
In fact, I thought that one of the things I would talk about today is “terroir”, which is
the French word that means the place, the geography, the soil, the climate, and the
people who are involved i n making the wine. It does not really have a literal English
translation. I have heard it described in a New Zealand context with the Māori word
“tūrangawaewae”—a place to stand. I think that is quite appropriate, but in the sense
that wine consumers can a nd do recognise styles of wine and where they come from by
the taste. The greats, like sauvignon blanc, chardonnay, and Pinot noir, are grown all
around the world, but New Zealand Marlborough sauvignon blanc is a unique product
and it has a unique taste to  it. That comes from the terroir. Even though you can isolate
different flavours down to a part of a vineyard, a Marlborough sauvignon blanc is quite
distinctive and is easily picked up by other people around the world who know exactly
what that is.
It is  really important that this bill is passed so that those customers and their
consumers can have confidence that when they pick up a bottle with “Marlborough” on
the label, that is what it will be. Likewise, with Central Otago Pinor noir. It also has its
own unique terroir, and you could also say the same for a Hawke’s Bay syrah. So all of
those flavours are important to people, and they are prepared to pay. My colleague
across the House, Mr Faafoi, likes his Scotch whisky —allegedly, well, he said so —and
the same principle applies, allegedly.
I think that all these things come back to why the wine industry is so successful.
Given that we are in the midst of the Trans -Pacific Partnership agreement ratification, I
should mention that the reason that the wine i ndustry is so successful, and why we need
these geographical indications passed in law, goes back to CER being passed, when the
wine industry had to face the harsh winds of competition, and it really made the wine
industry fit for exporting because it had to deliver what the customers wanted. Rather
than just producing a wine that people had no choice about they had to buy what was
available; it did not matter where it was grown —the industry then had to focus on the
consumer, and that is when all of our uni que terroirs were actually discovered. Rather
9904 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
than just being able to grow grapes, they were able to grow grapes that made wines that
were distinctive. So that is what led to that.
The New Zealand, South Island, and North Island geographical indications, which
will be an enduring part of this bill, are important because if there is a weather event and
a wine company needs more grapes to actually make its wine, it can still have a
geographical indications of the South Island if all the grapes are sourced from within the
South Island, or New Zealand if the grapes come from across the islands. So that is a
really important trade point. It will be very important that that comes in with the bill.
Likewise, having a renewal of the geographical indications every 1 0 years gives an
opportunity to push boundaries out or pull them back in if that is required as time goes
on.
It has been a great pleasure to support this bill. It has been a long time coming, and I
have been waiting since 2005, I think, when we really st arted talking about this, until
today. So it is with great pleasure that I commend this bill to the House. Thank you.

This is an important piece of legislation in an intellectual property sense and in a

It is interesting. I know we do have a number of connoisseurs in the House. I know,

I think there is more that we c an do and, perhaps, more that New Zealand Trade and

When he comes back to New Zealand, he enjoys it.
Not only is it a great industry and not only is there a bit  of fun and humour around it

are exposed to that. Our diplomatic folk, in all seriou sness, do a lot to promote the

I think this legislation is important to protect those brands. I think it is important in

It is a business where you have got to put a lot of capital out, you have got to spend a lot

9906 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
their shirt to grow a business, employ people, and provide a world -class, flagship export

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: That effort by the
Hon Clayton Cosgrove is going to be a little hard to follow be cause, being one who
favours drinking beer myself, I do not know the names of the wines quite as closely as

Ōhaupō in my electorate, which had a fire in the last 12 mon ths and has literally risen
from the ashes, rebuilt itself, and got going again.
It is a pleasure today to speak on this bill. New Zealand wines do attract a premium
in the overseas market and we do need to preserve and build on this. I want to make
note of the fact that for 20 consecutive years, year on year, the wine industry has had an
increase in export value. I think that it is pretty impressive, by anybody’s standards
from any industry, that it has been able to do that. When we talk about geographic
indications in relation to wine, it is important to note that we have 550,000 wine tourists
in this country. The definition of a wine tourist is a tourist who visits a winery; it is not
a definition of how much they consume when they go there. But it is rea lly important to
notice that if we have got 550,000 people coming to visit our wineries in New Zealand
and they spend almost, I understand, $3 billion —which was a 2015 figure—then people
are interested in the geographical specifics of where our wine comes from.
This bill is actually replacing or updating the principal Act, which was passed in
2006 but was never enacted for the reason that my colleague Stuart Smith explained

I think it is important to note that in this legislation the geographical indication will
