items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on this Geographical
Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment Bill. We will be supporting it.
The heart of this bill is about maintaining the integrity of New Zealand wine and
protecting the hard-won reputations of wine from the good wine -growing regions from
being undermined by inferior products usurping their names.
It is part of a wider thing, really, of appreciation by many consumers for products
from a single origin —for example, single -origin chocolate and single -origin coffee are
an incredibly different taste experience from the mass -produced commodities. And it is
similarly the case with wine. You can have a very different consumer experience and
appreciation when you learn to sample wines from different geographical areas. The
geographical indications are a way of telling a story about that product: about the region
that it comes from, about the soil that it has been grown in, about the weather that
produces that particular flavour of wine —and it is also why the vintage of wine and
taste will change from year to year, because the weather changes from year to year —
and about all of the other people who grow the wine. All of that is captured in
geographical indications as a way of furthering the relationships between the consumers
and the product. That is something that the Green Party is right behind. It is about
building a relationship between consumers and products, and the people who produce
17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9907
those products and the area where those products comes from. It is important to really
build that awareness.
Geographical indication is just one way of helping to build that awareness amongst
consumers for the product, and alongside that, people often want to know  about the
history of the region. I remember being quite fascinated with single -origin chocolate—
discovering where the cocoa beans had been grown and who grew them and how they
were transported here to New Zealand to be made into single -origin chocolate. That has
opened my eyes to a whole other way of relating to the products that we consume.
I think it is exactly the same for tourists who come to New Zealand and tour the
wineries. They can then develop an appreciation of where the wine that they are
drinking has come from, why it might taste and have the flavours that it does, and why
it will be distinctive to that area, and all of this is building individuality and uniqueness
as part of bringing value -added products to the primary production sector. That i s
something that we really want to be maintaining, not trying to compete in a sort of
mass-produced, anonymous commodities market, where it does not matter where the
product has come from, it is all been blended to be standardised, and all the uniqueness
and variation has been taken out. That is not the way that we should be building our
economy.
Our economy should be built on diversification and on relationships between the
consumers and the product that they are consuming and purchasing, and an
understanding and appreciation of where it comes from. With that understanding and
appreciation of the uniqueness of the product that they are consuming, there is very
often a willingness to pay a premium for that product because consumers have built that
relationship, and that is something that we need to be maximising. That is what this bill
is doing, and that is why we absolutely support it.
There is one important amendment that is included in this bill that I think is
incredibly important. It now stipulates that the 15 percent of the wine that does not
come from the geographical area still has to come from New Zealand. I think that is an
incredibly important amendment. It would be extremely bizarre to go through all this
effort to create a unique geographical indi cation and brand for an area and then dilute
that with imported wine. So it is absolutely wonderful that this has been included in this
bill. With that, it is a pleasure to support the bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am pleased to rise on behalf of New Zealand
First to take a call in this first reading of the Geographical Indications (Wine and
Spirits) Registration Amendment Bill. New Zealand First will be supporting this bill’s
referral to the select committee. This is an area of particular interest to me, being a
winemaker by trade, and I am sure it will be of particular interest to Mr Stuart Smith
when we come to consider the bill at the Primary Production Committee, under the most
able and affable chairmanship of Mr McKelvie.
Good things take time, and good wine is no exception. It would seem —or, at least, I
would hope, because it certainly seems the case —that good legislation is no exception
either. I say that because the genes is of this amendment bill lies in the primary Act,
which is the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Act 2006. The
explanatory note of this bill says that the primary Act was enacted in 2006 but never
brought into force. I am grateful f or the explanation that Mr Smith gave about the
reasons why it was not enacted at the time, because it did seem a little bit like making
hay while the sun was shining. I wondered whether, perhaps, back in 2006 things were
going so well that Parliament was not very busy. Maybe the House was up to speed with
everything and the Government did not have much to do, and, on that basis, it thought it
could enact a few laws and just have them on the back -burner, waiting to be brought
9908 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
into force if and when there wa s a rainy day and it needed to be done in a hurry. But I
digress a little.
The Act was never brought into force, and now that it is about to be, we have
discovered that there are a few things that are not quite right with it. There are things
that need to  be remedied and brought up to speed, as it were, before we bring the Act
out of mothballs, dust it off, and fire it up. Hence, we are here, debating this amendment
bill. It is not a monumental piece of legislation. It is not going to set the world on fire . I
very much doubt that the 6 o’clock news, on either channel, will run this as a headline.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Well, I don’t know.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Well, you say that, but you never know.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: It’s been a quiet week.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: It has not been that quiet, I think. But, nevertheless, it is an
important piece of legislation and it is important that we get it right. So, to do that, we
need to understand why it has come about and what the reasoning and purposes for it
are. We will pull all this to bits again in the select committee. We will examine the
entrails of the original legislation, and so forth.
But there is no substitute for going back to the beginning.  When I discovered that the
Act had been lurking around for 10 years, my curiosity was piqued somewhat. So I went
back into the archives. I went back and had a look at the Hansard from when the
original legislation was introduced. It is intriguing, looking  back 10 years into Hansard
and seeing some of the names that pop out of the pages. Some who have been in the
House a long time will remember them, and many who were outside the House but
followed the proceedings of the House will remember them. They are n ames that were
household names back then, walking the corridors of power, and so many of them are
not here any more, but some still are.
The Hon Judith Tizard was the Associate Minister of Commerce at the time and
moved the original bill, back in December  2005. It was 13 December, which, quite by
coincidence—at least, I imagine it is by coincidence —was the 363 rd anniversary of the
day that Abel Tasman first sighted New Zealand. I mention this because it would not
have occurred to Captain Tasman back then t hat perhaps three and a half centuries later
the legislature of the islands that he was looking at for the first time would be debating a
bill to give recognition to geographical indications of areas that might possibly be
bearing his name. I doubt that th e Hon Judith Tizard gave that possibility very much
thought, either. In fact, her speech, from the files of Hansard, gives no indication that
that may have been the case.
She did, however, outline the purpose of the bill, which was “to put in place a
modern, efficient, and cost -effective process for the registration of geographical
indications of wines and spirits, which both serves the purposes of our industries and
meets our obligations under the TRIPs agreement.” The TRIPs agreement is the World
Trade O rganization’s Agreement on Trade -Related Aspects of International Property
Rights. The Minister went on to outline quite a bit more about what the bill was
intended for and why it would be a very good thing for Parliament to pass it.
It was not to everyon e’s satisfaction, I have to say, because she was followed by a
certain Dr the Hon Lockwood Smith, who began his contribution by expressing
frustration at what he perceived was the Minister’s lack of understanding of the bill. He
chastised her, in the inimi table way that Dr Smith did —and I presume still does —for
gabbling and for not having the “faintest notion” of what the bill was about. He roundly
castigated her for her lack of proper pronunciation. Mr Assistant Speaker, I am sure you
will appreciate, as w ill others in the House, that when you have been castigated by
Lockwood Smith for improper pronunciation, you certainly know you have been
castigated.
17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9909
But he did support the bill. He expressed the National Opposition’s support for it —
get used to that term , gentlemen—as did Mr Doug Woolerton from the New Zealand
First Party, in his inimitable, laconic style, and also Keith Locke and Shane Jones, but
not the Māori Party. I found this quite intriguing. Before he was an “Hon”, Dr Pita
Sharples railed against the bill. He said that it breached the Treaty. He began his speech,
actually, by saying it was going to contribute to the extermination of the tuatara. It all
seemed to make sense as his speech unfolded. He proclaimed that his party’s opposition
to the bill  was on the basis of the recognition of tino rangatiratanga. So I will be
fascinated to see whether or not the Māori Party supports this amendment bill. Perhaps
there is enough in it, enough that has been changed, to change the minds of the Māori
Party mem bers. Maybe they will find it within themselves to revisit that original
opposition.
So here we find ourselves, in the 51 st Parliament, bringing modification to an Act
that was originally initiated by the 48 th Parliament, and some of the changes that the
amendment bill brings about are technical and some are minor. There is nothing, as I
say, earth-shattering—there is nothing in here that I can see, in the first reading, that we
will violently oppose. There are some questions, obviously, that I will look fo rward to
examining, as I say, in greater detail in the select committee. The fixed term for a
geographical indication, limiting it to 10 years with an ongoing right of renewal, is
obviously a feature of this amendment. It may be a good thing, or it might j ust be a
cynical ploy to extract even more in the way of fees from an industry that is already
horribly overburdened with taxes and levies and duties, but I will reserve judgment on
that until we have had submissions from the submitters to the select committee.
The provisions relating to the origin of wine we certainly agree with, in that the 85
percent requirement for grapes to have been grown in the particular geographical
location remains, but it also enforces the requirement for the other 15 percent to  be, at
least, from New Zealand. It is one thing to say that a Pinot noir is a Central Otago Pinot
noir if 85 percent of the grapes were grown in Central Otago and the other 15 percent
were perhaps grown in Waipara, but it is quite another matter to call i t a Central Otago
Pinot noir when the other 15 percent —one-sixth of the wine, in fact —were grown in
Chile, Tasmania, Bulgaria, or anywhere else.
So at this stage I do not intend to take too much more of the House’s time, but I
reiterate that New Zealand F irst will support this bill’s referral to the select committee
and, very probably, beyond. I look forward to examining it there, particularly regarding
the safety of the tuataras. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: That was just a very riveting
piece of history there from Mr Prosser. It was quite entertaining. I did read somewhere,
though, that Abel Tasman was a beer drinker, but I am not what the relevance is to this
piece of legislation.
Before I begin, I just want to acknowledge the representatives from the winegrowers’
association who are here in support of this bill, and the reason why I wanted to do that is
that I understand that there was an industry -wide push to have this piece of legislation
and, as Mr Prosser said, it has been a long time in the making. So I just want to
acknowledge the industry for its contribution to that. I also want to acknowledge the
Minister—who is no longer in the House—who is leading this bill, Paul Goldsmith—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: —for his work on this, as well as Tim Groser, who is obviously
no longer—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just interrupt the
member and give him a bit of friendly advice. Do not refer to the absence of members,
even nicely.
9910 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. So, getti ng back to the bill,
the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment Bill, as we
know, it provides a mechanism for the registration of the geographical indicators for
wine and spirits. Essentially, this enables the identification of wine and spirits as
originating from a particular region or a country or an area of the world, and,
representing an electorate that has a small but significant wine -growing and wine
business population with areas of Central Otago —particularly the Gibbston Valley—I
say this is pretty important. I think it has already been remarked that New Zealand is
very well regarded for various aspects of its wine, particularly its sauvignon blanc. But
Central Otago Pinot noir is also very highly regarded, and anything we can do to protect
the integrity of our premium brand and our reputation as a premium exporter, and just
the reputation that we have as a producer of products with a constant level of high
quality, is really important. I think this legislation is critical in that regard, particularly
as we embark on the further export of wine products.
We have seen that, dating back to just 1990 —the year I was born —our wine export
value was almost insignificant. It was almost nothing, and today it is worth up to about
$1.5 billion. That is huge, and the indications show that further exportation is going to
take place and the industry is going to continue to grow. As we look to compete more
head-on with various competitors across the world, maintaining that integrity and the
reputation of our products is going to be incredibly important. Effectively, 79 percent of
our wine is exported, and about a third of that is exported to the US. With the signing of
the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement, the tariff savings will also be a contributing
factor in opening up that market for our wines.
As I have said, the integrity and reputation and the confidence, as well, that
consumers have in what they are buying as being genuine products of New Zealand, or
genuine products of Central O tago, Marlborough, Martinborough, or wherever, are
going to be increasingly important as we look to compete at the premium level. The
tourism number of around 550,000 wine tourists coming to New Zealand last year is
significant, and it is significant in the Queenstown part of my electorate, as well. We see
an increasing number of visitors who are well educated in the wine space coming to
New Zealand, and if they feel like they are not getting the genuine product when they
are purchasing wine, then that coul d have a detrimental effect when they go back home
and talk to their colleagues and associates about their travel plans.
So, as a member of the Primary Production Committee, it is a great pleasure to
commend this bill to the House. I look forward to following it through the parliamentary
process, participating in that, and listening to all of the organisations and individuals
who have got a view on this piece of legislation. Thank you.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I rise to speak to the Geographical Indications
(Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment Bill. I come from Marlborough. I am
pleased to hear that there are wine industry people in the gallery above me who are
very, very keen to see this bi ll passed. It is an interesting one, however, that although
we acknowledge the provenance that is behind this bill, which is the absolute issue of
markets recognising where stuff comes from—the paddock-to-plate - type scenario—we
actually need to support t his all the way. So we need to be sure that the product that we
are going to put a name to actually will not negatively impact on the reputation of the
regions that we will be using the names of. What I am referring to is the issue of big
pesticide use, labour issues, and other social aspects that go with the industrialisation of
the wine industry in my region.
When we are having eels, or tuna, killed in a stream —200 of them recently —
probably by glyphosate spraying, is it the council or is it from adjacent,  overseas-owned
vineyards? If we are going —and we must go —down this track, then we must clean up
17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9911
the act of the wine industry around it. There is some really good news stuff from the
wine industry too, and that is that it wants to be 20 percent organic by 2020. That is a
step in the direction of cleaning up some of the reputation that it has had before.
Stuart Smith may chortle, but this spring —and I have said it in the House before and
I have said it to the industry before —just as in 2007, the member over  there who is
chortling had 100 percent vineyard herbicide coverage in spring to crank up his soil
temperatures, using a non -sustainable method. But that can get a sustainable wine -
growing tick. It is nuts. There is nothing sustainable about having 100 per cent of your
surface area sprayed with herbicide every spring, and, of course, we know that we have
got herbicide resistance with ryegrass in Marlborough from repeated spraying. So I
support this bill, and our party is going to support this bill, but the r eputation in our
markets is not through having bulk pesticide and herbicide spraying.
I know that there is work done to make sure that there is little, if any, residue of
pesticides in the sprays, and it is important that we make sure that products going to
market are as clean as possible. They can be cleaner, and so can the environment in my
region, where we have tuna dying from pesticides, where we are getting spray resistance
from herbicides, and where we have a lot of people getting sick, but we cannot  quite put
the finger on why. The pesticides invariably used are carcinogenic or probable
carcinogens, as the World Health Organization says for glyphosate. Others are
endocrine disrupters or neurotoxins.
We can improve the health of my region, Hawke’s Bay, and the other regions where
we are growing a lot of grapes. It is a fantastic industry —it is doing us proud at the
moment, in terms of economic benefit—but it needs to convert to doing a lot better than
the so-called sustainable wine-growing that is actually almost a crock of the proverbial.
Yes, it is integrated pest management, and it is not spraying every 2 calendar weeks or
whatever—there is a certain level of monitoring and decision making around it —but it
is a choice of what products are used when there is a pest outbreak. It is an issue of what
systems are being used.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has
concluded.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call in
support of the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment
Bill. I would like to acknowledge speakers who have gone before and t he contribution
from New Zealand First with some of the history of this. It has been a week in this
House of bonhomie and consensual decision -making, and this is not the first bill that
has gone through with, most probably, unanimous support. I guess that is what the
public likes to see —Parliament speaking with one voice. The last one was about
protecting fish in the Kermadec Islands, and in respect of this one you might say some
people drink in that way. This will improve the quality of the perception of o ur wine.
Amongst other things, it will require geographical indications that will go from 85
percent to 100 percent of the grapes for the wine coming from the regions that are on
the indication, and that is a good thing—a good thing.
There is an interesti ng history for this bill. The original Act was passed in 2006 by
the Hon Judith Tizard. It lay in a veritable legislative stupor. It was not actually set up,
and now we are back 10 years later to give it a kick along and improve it with the
amendment. I think we are all probably of the same mind that the industry has come of
age and it is time to lift the bar on geographical indications to 100 percent. So that is
good and we expect that when this bill goes through, with the broad support of the
House, the implementation steps will be taken.
We will get such great names as “North Island”, “South Island”, and “New Zealand”
thrown in, and then beyond that it is going to be up to the regions to define and agree on
9912 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
their geographical indications. So for members opposite they will have a great interest
in Marlborough, Martinborough, Hokonui in the case of the member for Southland —
God knows what it is going to come up with —and Central Otago. He is a member who
has got a vast swathe of Southland and a little, tiny w eeny bit of Central Otago so that
he can do his odd weekend clinic in the vineyards, so I guess that is a fair
apportionment. We all smile because this subject matter brings to mind some of the
finer parts of recreation and life in New Zealand.
I do want to acknowledge the wine industry—the viticulture industry. There are a lot
of hard -working people there doing very well. They have had their ups and downs.
Grape prices collapsed a few years ago and they have recovered, a bit like dairy being
down at the m oment. There has been a lot of consolidation in the industry. There are a
few people who went to set up vineyards and their own wine labels as a kind of lifestyle
choice or retirement hobby and it has turned out to be bloody hard work, and there has
been a lot of consolidation to group that into more economic unit sizes. But it is a high -
quality industry. New Zealand wine can hold its head up very high by international
standards, and, arguably, there is no finer sauvignon blanc grown in the world than that
which comes from Marlborough in New Zealand. I have yet to taste a Pinot noir that I
prefer to the one from good old Central Otago.
I want to acknowledge Waipara, which is doing extremely well, and Martinborough,
as well as Hawke’s Bay and other regions. We have, of course, in west Auckland —
where I have the privilege of being an MP —a fine tradition of the Dalmatian
winemakers. There are the Babiches, the Brajkoviches, and many others who have come
up with brands like Nobilo Wines, Soljans Estate Winery, an d Kūmeu River, which
makes some of the world’s very finest chardonnay, and we are very proud of that
tradition in the west.
Of course Labour will be supporting this bill. We commend the bill to the House. We
look forward to its, I think, unanimous passage  and, along with the Kermadec fish
reserve, we look forward to many more years of research of the product. Thank you
very much.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise to speak to the Geographi cal
Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment Bill —I just wanted to make
sure that I could actually say it without stumbling over the words, for a start. Coming
from Palmerston North, I have got to say that I am very much used to the importance  of
trading off a good name for a geographical location. So it is something that is dear to
my heart—the importance of actually being able to stand by your geographical location,
and being able to trade off that. However, when it comes to wine, I have to
acknowledge that I am not as learned as Mr Faafoi or any of my colleagues on this side.
In fact, probably, I am just one step above philistine when it comes to my knowledge of
wine. But what I absolutely am committed to is this Government being absolutely 1 00
percent behind our exporters —100 percent behind those who are doing very well —and
helping them to ensure that their success continues to grow.
In 1990, as my colleague Mr Barclay said earlier, the wine export industry was
basically non-existent. I have brought a little graphical example—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: They have all been pulled
out.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: What was that?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: All the vines have been
pulled out. The Government paid a subsidy to pull vines out.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: Oh, OK. Anyway —thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker; I thought I
had done something wrong, which is normally when you i ntervene, but OK —in 1990
17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9913
the export wine industry was practically nil, and you can see a sharp increase on this
graph up to 2015, when we are now at over $1.5 billion in exports.
If we want our exporters to be successful —if we want them to continue to be
successful—we have got to make sure that our legislation continues to support and back
them. Giving them this ability to trade off their geographical location, to ensure that that
has some sound basis behind it so that the consumers can be confident that wh at they
are buying is, in fact, what it is that they are buying, is really important. No disrespect to
beer making, but clearly, obviously, it is not necessarily that important whether or not
Tui is manufactured in Mangatainoka, just around the corner from where I live.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: It is for them.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: It is for the people of Mangatainoka, clearly, but not necessarily
for the consumers.
I think I have said enough. There has been a good -humoured debate, obviously,
going on with this bill. But what this bill is going to do, I hope, is continue to allow this
graph to grow at the exponential rate that it already has over the last 25 years. I look
forward to seeing even greater wine exports from our country with the aid of thi s
legislation.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Happy St Patrick’s Day to
everybody.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: What’s a good Irish drop?

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: Oh, no. Nobody wo uld like me to tell my Irish jokes as we are
standing here tonight. I do think that mentioning St Patrick’s Day is important, given
the topic of conversation, and I hope we have all been having a little wine tonight,
talking about the wine and whisky. Befo re we get into the serious part of the bill, I
would say that I am a bit concerned about the spelling of the word “whisky” in this
discussion, as we will take it through the select committee. In my view, coming from an
Irish background—and, I think, on thi s particular day I am allowed to have an opinion
on this, and the opinion is allowed to be respected —whisky should be spelt with an “e”
and not just a “y”. So I just want to put that on the record for the House.
It is a curious thing to be debating an ame ndment to an Act that was passed 10 years
ago and was not enacted. It has been sitting in an un -enacted state—if there is such a
term—since then. It seems that the impetus for the amendment that we have before us
tonight, in this first reading, is an amend ment that has been driven by the wine industry
and imminent free -trade talks with the European Union, whereas 10 years ago that
impetus was not there, from the amount of reading that I have been able to do on the
bill. This impetus has now changed, and I t hink the member across the House, Jono
Naylor, who got up before me to speak, was, quite rightly, pointing out that the wine
industry is becoming an increasingly important part of our economy. I think,
somewhere in the regulatory impact statement, it might  have been, there is a prediction
that it is going to be $2 billion of value to our economy in the near future, and that is
clearly important. Our wine industry is a critical part of our economy, and we need to
ensure that we are doing the best that we can to protect it.
I know we are talking about geographical indications, which is a curious phrase, and,
no doubt, one that we will all become very familiar with over the passage of this bill. I
am certainly keen for the geographical indication of Central Otago to become a meme,
and for that to be a powerful meme, as I am sure it is in our export markets, with our
major export markets being Europe and Australia and the US, as I understand it, for
wine. This bill seemed to come up again with a survey that was done by the Ministry for
Primary Industries last year, and there were a number of submissions on that, and a
number of options that are set out in the regulatory impact statement, around how it
should be dealt with again.
9914 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016
As I said, the impetus for this seems to have come from the wine industry itself
around ensuring that it is protected in the European market. So Labour is supporting this
bill’s referral to the select committee because we think that this needs to be looked at
again. But, as no doubt othe r speakers have canvassed through the afternoon, there are
some substantial changes in this amendment bill to the original legislation from 10 years
ago, in 2006, with the major amendment being to increase the percentage of local —
being New Zealand—grapes in wine to 100 percent, as opposed to 85 percent. That was
the option that was recommended following that survey and in the regulatory impact
statement. I think that is clearly something that will be debated in the select committee,
as to what the implications of that are and what the risks are of sticking with the existing
legislation, which is 85 percent. I think they used the phrase “cross -country blending”
risks as being one of the major reasons for making that substantial change from the
2006 legislatio n, and also the potential for abuse of wines being created in other
countries that are labelled as being “in the style of” —for example, Central Otago Pinot
noir or Marlborough sauvignon blanc or whatever. I am only going to talk about the
South Island, bec ause that is what really matters when it comes to geographical
indications.
What is curious —and this is what I would like to tease out a bit more as we go
through the discussion on this bill —is that when this legislation was enacted in 2006 it
was enacted  at a time, according to the regulatory impact statement, “when it was
expected that negotiations would soon begin on a Wine Agreement with the EU.
Negotiations were never started, and at the time, the New Zealand wine industry did not
support the implementation of [this legislation]. As a result, [it] was never brought into
force.” So I think what we have to do is some catch -up around that: why things have
changed, what the benefits are now, what will actually occur as a result of bringing this
legislation into force, whether there will be any costs —well, of course there will be
costs, but what the implications of those costs will be and whether they will be costs
primarily to the industry—the extent to which there will be a bureaucratic system that is
set up to keep a register of the geographical indications, what that will involve, and the
pros and cons of that around the benefits to the wine industry, generally, and to our
trade relationships, with the European Union particularly, as a consequence. So I a m
looking forward to that.
I am also looking forward to —quickly, Mr Assistant Speaker —any innovation that
occurs as a result of at least having the discussion, and possible legislative outcomes, on
this around tracing. I think this is a really important a rea of innovation for food and
wine and any other beverages and produce from New Zealand around the innovative
technologies that are emerging around tracing what you eat, where it comes from,
including the history, the soil quality, the geographical surrou ndings, etc. There is a lot
of movement happening in this area. Fish is a good example of that. If you go into a
restaurant anywhere in the world and you buy a fish that has come from New Zealand,
there is the potential for you to be able to then trace whe re that fish came from, where it
was caught, when it was caught, what the circumstances were of it being caught, and
what the surrounding environment was like. That is value -adding for New Zealand food
and beverages, and I think that this legislation is ta king a step in that direction in
marketing the importance to the world of the wine industry, the grapes, and the amazing
environment in which they are grown. That can only be a good thing, so we are
supporting this bill’s referral to the select committee.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: I am taking a very short call to support the
Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment Bill in its first
reading. It is really good to see the support for this bill.
17 Mar 2016 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 9915
Just this morning I was in a meeting attended by my colleagues and some business
people who are exporting 95 percent of their products. I asked them what the value of
Made in New Zealand was to them, and the answer was th at it is huge. So this bill is
about adding that value to our wine and spirit products. The reputation of products that
are made here in New Zealand is important to us, and if the geographical origin of wine
and spirit products is registered, giving a clea r indication of the specific region it is
coming from, that will give confidence not only to consumers but also to makers,
because then they can claim a special place in the market, especially the export market.
I do not drink, but I understand it is very important for those who do drink. I support
this bill and commend this bill to the House. Thank you.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Primary Production Committee.
Third Reading
Debate resumed from 10 March.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: I last spoke about this bill last
Thursday night. Just to recap very briefly, we are addressing the passage of a bill that
has been sitting on the Order Paper since 2009, following a review of the Radio New
Zealand charter that took place in 2005—so this is 11 years after a review took place.
There is a statutory requirement for a review of the Radio New Zealand charter to
occur every 5 years. In essence, we have skipped two reviews. Therefore, by the time
the legislation before us tonight is actually pas sed, it may be out of date. I want to put
that on the record. I think that what that represents is the lack of commitment that the
Government has shown towards public broadcasting in this country, and its disdain for
ensuring that we are keeping up to date , and taking seriously Radio New Zealand’s role
in how our democracy functions and the importance of public broadcasting for public
debate and commercial-free discussion and programming.
Radio New Zealand operates in very difficult circumstances. As a res ult, it has been
under a funding freeze since 2009. It is doing the best job it can, and that job is pretty
good. It is making the transition to multimedia broadcasting, and it is doing that in
difficult circumstances. Unfortunately, the chair of Radio New  Zealand revealed to a
select committee a couple of weeks ago that it would not be making a funding bid in
this Budget. That is very disappointing and sad, quite frankly, but whatever. Radio New
Zealand is also undergoing restructuring while it adapts to a  multimedia environment,
and that has created some pain within the organisation.
We support this legislation; we support the review that took place. We know that the
minute this legislation gets passed, Radio New Zealand is, no doubt, going to go into
another cycle of a review, so it kind of makes a farce of the whole process.
We also note that the Minister of Broadcasting submitted a substantial amendment in
the Committee stage and did not speak to that amendment until briefly in the third
reading. The e ssence of that was to make provision for multi -platform provisions and
for the generation of new content-related revenue streams overseas, assuming that it can
find any buyers. It is a bit like the BBC versus BBC World Service, where the
commercial arm gen erates revenue but the core services are still subject to public
service provisions. However, Radio New Zealand does not have any plans at this point
that we know of to generate revenue in that way, and it is very constricted by its current
funding environment.
9916 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 17 Mar 2016
Lastly, I would like to put on the record that there is a member’s bill in the ballot
called the Radio New Zealand (Catch -up Funding) Amendment Bill, which does
increase funding for Radio New Zealand by around 20 to 25 percent, using inflation and
population growth as the way to make those adjustments. This would make a difference
and would ensure that this bill actually does have some meaning when it finally is
enacted, by making Radio New Zealand the efficient, meaningful organisation and
provider of value to the New Zealand community that it should be, and ensuring that it
is properly funded. Unfortunately, this bill before the House tonight rings hollow
because of the situation that Radio New Zealand finds itself in.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to take a call on the final
reading of the Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill. Before I actually get to the
substance of the speech, I just want to respond to the comments that wer e made by Ms
Curran. Having been a broadcaster myself—having actually worked for Television New
Zealand and having actually run a production company —sometimes having more
money does not necessarily mean better quality. I am a proponent of local content and  I
think that has been put on the record. I support the work that the great many people in
this country actually do to create local content, and I celebrate that, but more money
does not necessarily mean better quality.
This side of the House has been comm itted to ensuring that the New Zealand Public
Service delivers more for the country, and this includes the continuing support of our
public radio broadcast service, a service that is reliable and consistent for today’s
listeners. The bill we are debating t oday will make a stronger statement about our plan
to support good independent broadcasting. The bill, of course, has the Radio New
Zealand charter as one of its core components. The charter states that the purpose of
Radio New Zealand is to be a public br oadcaster that works for all New Zealanders. It
also provides a number of provisions that indicate how the broadcaster is able to deliver
this admirable goal.
We are now entering a new age of public broadcasting where many New Zealanders
are now going onli ne to listen to podcasts of Radio New Zealand shows, from home to
work and at leisure. Often I think a lot of people rely on the app that they have on their
mobile phones to listen to Radio New Zealand as well, and I commend the work of
Radio New Zealand for creating a great app for the convenience of its listeners.
More New Zealanders from different walks of life are also tuning in to listen. They
are no longer listening to the programmes on the end of the old radio transmitter. They
are also doing it time  shifted, as well —not only are they listening but they are also
watching pictures on radio. I have seen many radio shows where they include pictures.
In the old days, when we were talking about radio, it was radio with sound but without
pictures, and when we talked about television, it was just pictures with sound, right? But
now there is a convergence in the medium, and radio often also has pictures, as well. It
is modern technology that is actually providing that.
It is also important to remember that mos t New Zealanders are no longer waiting for
announcements—as I said, we are time shifting. Busy lifestyles mean that we are never
actually in one place tuning in at the right time, waiting for that broadcast. Throughout
the last week, Radio New Zealand had a number of programmes that let us discover new
and exciting stories about our country and the world we live in. I look forward to seeing
what new ideas its production team has coming up in the near future.
Members should also remember the role of Radio Ne w Zealand as a lifeline during
times of natural disaster. Radio New Zealand was a key service many Cantabrians
looked to during the aftermath of the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes. The role of Radio
New Zealand as a support entity with obligations to the Minist ry of Civil Defence and
17 Mar 2016 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 9917
wider emergency services must also be noted by the House as a key component of the
community support role that it provides.
Radio New Zealand, as a broadcaster, has over 500,000 listeners a week, comprising
nearly 20 percent of the market share of audience. These numbers show how highly
regarded the broadcaster is in New Zealand, and I celebrate that.
I should also note to the House that the Commerce Committee, which I chair,
recently reviewed Radio New Zealand during our annual rev iew process, and it was
great to hear about its current operations and how it seeks to tackle future changes in
technology, and also the listening habits of the audiences. It was also interesting to note
how it is looking into the ethnic diversity of New Z ealand’s population. It was looking
into more representation in terms of programming representing the ethnic diversity, as
well as the content for the younger generation in the digital age.
Indeed, the Commerce Committee has had a long history with the bil l, as members
opposite have actually mentioned. It began the hearings in 2009, and it is appropriate
that now, 6 years later, this House can send a strong message to the nation about our
belief in what the Radio New Zealand services should be achieving for the people of our
country.
As members of Parliament we have a duty to New Zealand to maintain Radio New
Zealand as a key broadcaster for this country. We also have the duty to help the
Government fulfil its responsibilities towards Radio New Zealand. Thes e
responsibilities can be fulfilled only through our recognition of the digital era we are in
and the impact that it will have on the traditional mediums that, for a long time, Radio
New Zealand has operated under. This bill actually works for changes and looks ahead
to the future vision of our nation so that Radio New Zealand can continue to be a good
public broadcast service. In summary, Radio New Zealand is well trusted and will
remain so in our country, and I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: It is a genuine pleasure to speak to the Radio
New Zealand Amendment Bill, and I want to acknowledge Melissa Lee, the speaker
who has just made a contribution, who is the chair of the C ommerce Committee, and
who, as she pointed out herself, was a broadcaster and —importantly, I think —a
broadcaster who was making her own programmes in that creative space. So she does
know what she is talking about when we are talking about the broadcasting  industry at
large.
I also want to acknowledge the people who work for Radio New Zealand. I think
that—and it has been mentioned on this side of the House —given the financial
constraints that it is under and the digital change that the whole industry is u ndergoing,
it has responded to those digital changes and the financial challenges in a very effective
way. But I think it could have been better, and that speaks to our disappointment about
the passage of this bill. I think that if you look at the details of the bill itself and the
functions of this bill, you have to say it is a good bill because it puts in legislation the
charter for Radio New Zealand and it enshrines some very important things, in my
view, as a former broadcaster who spent most of his tim e in public broadcasting. Radio
New Zealand, by law, has to deliver services of the highest quality to inform, entertain,
and enlighten the people of New Zealand, to challenge, innovate, and engage its
listeners, and to foster crucial thought and informed and wide -ranging debate. As a
citizen and as a former broadcaster, I think that those functions are very good functions
and are ones that, hopefully, we all support.
Unfortunately, the last words in this piece of legislation tell the sorry story of the
journey of this bill. Melissa Lee pointed out in her contribution that this piece of
legislation was introduced on 2 June 2009, and we are here —and there is a degree of
hypocrisy here on my part, because we are speaking to it and it has taken so long and
9918 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 17 Mar 2016
there have been so many delays, but I think it is important that we point this out. I do
not want to overly prolong this debate —I want this piece of legislation to pass —but I
think it is important that we do point out that in 2009 this piece of legislation ca me out,
the select committee reported back in December of that year, and it has taken us 6 years,
as Melissa Lee pointed out herself, for this piece of legislation to pass. I think that
speaks to the priority that this Government has put on public broadcas ting, and I think
the 6-year wait shows that it is a low priority. It is dangerous, not only for some of the
functions that I spoke about that are enshrined for Radio New Zealand but also because
of the quickly changing nature of the media. If we want Radi o New Zealand, which, I
think, is our shining light of public broadcasting, to be just as good as the ever -changing
market with New Zealand Media and Entertainment, with Fairfax, with our other public
broadcaster, Television New Zealand, and with other med ia outlets in New Zealand, we
have to support our radio public broadcaster to make sure it can change with the times
and ensure that the high -quality standards that we expect, and that it delivers, can be
delivered as well.
Melissa Lee spoke about the convergence—that radio is no longer radio alone. On air
at the moment, I believe, is Checkpoint, and it is not just radio alone, now. John
Campbell, since leaving MediaWorks, now does his show online —you can watch him
do his show. That is why I want to congra tulate Radio New Zealand on branching out
into that area. But I think the financial constraints that this Government has put on
Radio New Zealand are restricting Radio New Zealand’s ability to do more. If we want
our public broadcaster to do more —to challenge, to inform, to have those debates that
the charter talks about, and to keep that quality —it also needs to be at the forefront of
technological changes. I think that the lack of commitment over those 6 years has
seriously hamstrung Radio New Zealand. I think you just need to look to Television
New Zealand and what the current Government has done there as well. Removing
TVNZ 6 and TVNZ 7, again, shows a lack of commitment to public broadcasting. I do
not know why, because I think it is an important thing for our nation to have scrutiny —
unbiased scrutiny with integrity —and I think that comes from having a public
broadcaster.
So when we look at this piece of legislation, the functions are great; the journey is
awful. Six years is too long to wait for this p iece of legislation to pass through this
House. A funding freeze since 2009 to keep it to just under $32 million for Radio New
Zealand is not good enough for what I would hope we are, which is a good, functioning
democracy.

RETIREMENTS 
Serjeant-at-Arms—Brent Smith 
Mr SPEAKER : Honourable members, most members will be aware that our 
Serjeant-at-Arms retires tomorrow, after 13 years in the role. I am sure that members 
would join with me in thanking Brent Smith for his service and in wishing him all the 
best for a well-earned retirement. [Applause] 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : I am not applying for the job, 
by the way. When the House resumes on Tuesday, 29 Marc h the Government will look 
to make progress on the New Zealand Business Number Bill and first readings of the 
New Zealand Horticultural Export Authority Amendment Bill and the Wildlife 
(Powers) Amendment Bill, and also progress on the Committee stages on t he Order 
Paper. 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Senior Whip —Labour): Mr Speaker, can I just, on behalf of 
the Opposition and in keeping with the statement you made at the beginning of question 
time today, add our thanks to Brent Smith for his 13 years of service to the House. I am 
told that in that time, he has taken only 1½ days of sick leave. So I hope that his 
successor will have a similar level of dedication and commitment to this House. 
Mr SPEAKER: I thank the member. 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Prime Minister, Statements—New Zealand Women Leaving for Syria and Iraq 
1. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister : Was he 
advised, prior to 8 December 2015, that the so called “jihadi brides” he referred to 
during the Intelligence and Security Committee meeting were a ll resident in Australia 
and did not leave from New Zealand? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House)  on behalf of the Prime 
Minister: Yes. 
Metiria Turei: So the Prime Minister can confirm that he knew that none of those 
women had left for Syria or Iraq from New Zealand? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE : Yes, and the member needs to be aware that as New 
Zealand citizens it does not matter where they left from . If they pose a security risk to 
New Zealand on their return, then that is something we are concerned about. 
Metiria Turei: Why did the Prime Minister not make it clear that these women did 
not leave from New Zealand when he said: “There’s , in my view, no question that there 
have been one or two people who have left and it would appear on all factors that we 
know that they are going as jihadi brides.”? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE : It was not actually the Prime Minister who answer ed 
the question, but what I can say is that where they leave from is irrelevant. They are 
New Zealand citizens, they may return to New Zealand, and they are of concern to us. 
Metiria Turei : Why did the Prime Minister not tell New Zealanders  that these 
women were living in Australia when the media were reporting that these women had 
left from New Zealand? 
9868 Oral Questions 17 Mar 2016 
 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE: I am unware of the media reports and not responsible 
for them. The reality is that they were travelling on New Zealand passports. 
Metiria Turei : If the Prime Minister knew that no women had left from New 
Zealand for Syria or Iraq for this purpose, why did he not give that information to the 
Islamic Women’s Council, which asked for evidence for his statements? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE : Where they left from is irrelevant. If they are New 
Zealanders then they are of concern to us. If they are posing a security risk because they 
may return to New Zealand, that is of concern to u s. Whether someone is in New 
Zealand or not does not remove their New Zealand citizenship —as we have recently 
found out. 
Metiria Turei : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was very clear: 
why did the Prime Minister not give information to an organisation when they asked for 
it? It was irrelevant—his answer. 
Mr SPEAKER : No, no, but the question was addressed by the Minister —
effectively, saying that where they left from was irrelevant. That was the way he chose 
to answer the question. He has addressed the question. 
Metiria Turei: Why did the Prime Minister allow the misinformation about where 
these women were living to carry on, and was it because he was wanting to build his 
case for increased spy agency powers? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE : No, the fact is that these women are New Zealand 
citizens, have travelled to Syria, and may pose a security risk to New Zealand on their 
return. 
Metiria Turei : Will the Prime Minister now ap ologise to the many Muslim 
women—[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The question can be asked. 
Metiria Turei: Will the Prime Minister now apologise to the many Muslim women 
whom he alienated when he misled the public into believing that women were leaving 
New Zealand to become jihadi brides? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE : No, because there is only one person in this House 
who has identified these people as being Muslim. I will make the other point that New 
Zealand citizens on a New Zealand passport going to Syria from another country left 
New Zealand at some point. 
Economy—Reports 
2. CHRIS BISHOP (National) to the Minister of Finance: What recent reports has 
he received on the New Zealand economy? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance : Statistics New Zealand has today reported that the ec onomy grew 0.9 
percent in the 3 months to December. This took annual growth over 2015 to 2.3 percent. 
The first half of 2015 was a weaker time for the economy, so it is pleasing to see that 
growth has picked up again in the second half of the year, with tw o quarters of nearly 1 
percent growth now. Growth was led by service industries, which made up 70 percent 
of the economy. The construction sector also saw strong growth. Our 0.9 percent 
growth rate compares positively with other developed countries, with 0 .6 percent in 
Australia, 0.5 percent in the UK, and 0.3 percent in the US. The OECD average was 0.3 
percent. 
Chris Bishop : How is diversification of the economy contributing to sustained 
moderate growth and delivering more jobs and higher in comes for New Zealand 
families? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : It is clear from these numbers that the New Zealand 
economy is proceeding in a diversified manner. We have a dairy industry that is having 
17 Mar 2016 Oral Questions 9869 
 
a difficult time at the moment, but, despite thi s, we are seeing solid growth, more 
employment, and higher wages. Although we are, of course, concerned for dairy 
farmers, the important lesson is that it does not mean that the whole economy is in 
difficulty. And that, frankly, is a good thing for all of New Zealand. We are seeing 
continued growth across many parts of the economy. For example, tourism is 
performing well; annual beef exports are now up one -third in the last year; international 
education was worth $3.1 billion in 2015 —and that supports 30,00 0 jobs —and wine 
exports are now worth $1.5 billion, up 14 percent in just 1 year. 
Grant Robertson: Do the latest GDP figures show the second consecutive quarter of 
falling per capita real disposable income? 
Hon STEVEN J OYCE: I congratulate the member, because he has obviously been 
in his office trying to find the one slightly negative statistic, ever since quarter to 11 this 
morning. Real GDP per capita, which the member used to care about, up until this 
week, has gone u p in both of the last two quarters. The real gross national disposable 
income per capita, which the member is now so fixed on, has gone down slightly in the 
latest figures. 
Grant Robertson: Was Westpac senior economist Michael Gordon wron g when he 
said that GDP growth per capita is “actually very sluggish at present.”? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: Speaking of sluggish—no, it is not. The September quarter 
and the December quarter are both at 0.3 or 0.4, from memory. 
Grant Robertson: So he’s wrong? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Well, the Westpac economists were predicting 7 percent 
unemployment this year at one stage. I note they have been very quiet on that lately. 
Chris Bishop: What reports has he received recently on reductions in New Zealand’s 
external financial vulnerabilities? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: It is good news there, too. Statistics New Zealand yesterday 
released its latest balance of payments figures. They showed a curre nt account deficit of 
3.1 percent, which, of course, is significantly better than we used to experience. We 
were around the 8 percent mark back in the period prior to the global financial crisis, 
before this Government came into office. Statistics New Zealand also reported that New 
Zealand’s net external debt has now fallen to 55 percent of GDP, down from 83 percent 
when National took office, and is now at the lowest level since 2003. These figures 
represent good progress in improving a longstanding imbalan ce in the New Zealand 
economy, which we inherited. Lower national debt means New Zealand is better placed 
to respond to any future economic shocks. 
Chris Bishop: How is the Government’s responsible and consistent programme of 
economic manage ment, which contrasts with reports of other, more knee -jerk 
approaches, supporting ongoing moderate growth in the economy? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: It is important that the Government continues to undertake 
responsible and consistent economic reform that gives businesses the confidence to 
invest and grow, and not just react to the latest news cycle. We are doing that, for 
example, through the Business Growth Agenda, which includes 350 initiatives, like 
signing up to new free -trade agreements, reducing ACC levies by around $1.5 billion a 
year, rolling out the ultra -fast broadband programme, and launching three new ICT 
graduate schools. This all translates into an outlook that is for continued economic 
growth. In fact, Treasury’s Half Year Economi c and Fiscal Update forecast growth 
averaging around 3 percent over calendar years 2016 and 2017, while the Reserve Bank 
forecast is similar for the next 2 years. 
9870 Oral Questions 17 Mar 2016 
 
Dairy Industry—Milk Price Downturn 
3. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of 
Finance: Does he stand by his reported statement from February this year that he is not 
overly concerned about the broader impact of the slump in dairy prices? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance : In the context in which it was made, yes. As I said earlier, there is a 
difference between being concerned for farmers, and being concerned that the dairy 
sector will drag the rest of the economy into recession. Of course, we have seen that that 
will not necessarily happen, because of the GDP figures today. Of course we are 
concerned about the welfare  of farmers, but this does not detract from the fact that we 
are seeing continued growth across the rest of the economy. Despite the fall in dairy 
prices, for example, exports actually increased by almost $2 billion for New Zealand 
last year and, as I ment ioned in the earlier question, tourism, beef exports, international 
education, and wine are just four examples of that growth.  
Grant Robertson : Is Waimate mayor Craig Rowley wrong when he says that the 
dairy downturn is going to have a “ massive onflow” in his town and that “There will be 
no winners. It’s a struggle for everybody.”, or should the people of Waimate not be 
overly concerned, either? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Obviously there are some towns that are being affected by  
the downturn in dairy prices. I can think of a number that I have visited in recent times

couple of weeks, where parties have come together to discuss the final shape of the

The genesis of the bill, though, started quite some time ago, when it was decided that 
there should be an orderly transition for the Government to exit some of its more 
prominent roles in th e recovery of Christchurch. So in December of 2014, under the 
chair of Dame Jenny Shipley, there was an advisory board set up. It was asked to 
consider a number of parameters that should be given a fair old going over before any 
transition plan could be pu t together, and then it was asked to produce a report that 
would indicate a direction moving forward.

District, the Mayor of Selwyn District, and the current chair of Enviro nment 
Canterbury, as well as people from the business sector and a number of people from the 
NGO sector, as well. The people who were on that board did, I think, a splendid job of 
thinking about the state of the city at present, particularly in a governanc e sense, and 
looking at what might be necessary moving forward. So what we have seen in the last 
10 days, when MPs have repeatedly met, discussed, and agreed, is a continuation of a 
consultation process that has gone on for a very long period of time. The arrangements 
that are now going to be presented in the Committee stage as a Supplementary Order 
Paper to this particular bill, when the House resumes after the adjournment, I think are

going to put into statute a series of arrangements that will work well for the future of the 
city.

broad consensus on how that should shape up, and I would like to take this opportunity 
to acknowledge the hard work, and actually the determined work, I should say, of all the 
MPs who were party to that. These were Denis O’Rourke from New Zealand First,

I am very pleased to take a call on the Greater Christchurch Regeneration Bill. As Mr

When the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act expires in April this year, with the 
extraordinary powers that it provides to the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake 
Recovery and the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority —or CERA —it is 
certainly the opportunity for a major step change in terms of who makes decisions and 
how those decisions are made about Christchurch’s future. Now that we are 5 years on 
from the devastating quakes in February 2011 and are over that emergency and 
immediate recovery phase, we do need to see a shift from central government to local 
leadership. Certai nly, the Local Government and Environment Committee did make 
some good changes to the bill as introduced, one of them being the way “regeneration” 
is defined. It includes, as Nicky Wagner noted, improving the environmental, economic, 
social, and cultural w ell-being and resilience of communities. That is a very positive 
change, particularly as the Government has stripped out from the purpose of local 
government the promotion of community well -being. It is really good to see that at the 
heart of this bill. 
But the Green Party opposed the bill as it came back from the select committee 
because it did not provide for a genuine partnership between central government and 
local authorities in planning and guiding the next stage of Christchurch’s post -
earthquake future. It contained far too many hangovers from the Canterbury Earthquake 
Recovery Authority era and from the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority 
legislation. It left far too much power with the executive and with central government 
Ministers and agencie s—particularly the Department of the Prime Minister and 
Cabinet—in their ability to initiate regeneration plans and then have the relevant 
Minister approve or decline those plans at the end of the process. This was particularly 
important because in this bi ll it is not just the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake 
Recovery who can exercise these decision-making and approval powers but it is also the 
relevant “Minister”, depending on the function being exercised —so that could be the 
Minister of Transport, or it could be the Minister for Land Information. 
That whole concentration of power at the centre was in total opposition to the strong 
and eloquent call by submitters during those 2½ days of hearings in Christchurch, and 
through written submissions, for local leadership, for a reduction in the power of central 
government and Ministers, and for a much stronger role for people in Christchurch. 
Certainly for me, it has been organisations like Greening The Rubble and Gap Filler, 
with their innovative, creative, com munity-orientated projects that have been inspiring 
in showing what Christchurch people are capable of. Some of the private buildings, 
which are quite innovative in their design and their construction, particularly where they 
use our local resource —wood—show what can happen in Christchurch when we have 
local people making those decisions. It is especially important, too, when we have had 
democracy denied to the Canterbury region with the half -pie, half -appointed, half -
elected model that we have got at Environment Canterbury. 
This bill did need to establish a framework and a structure for decision making that 
put Regenerate Christchurch as this new agency that is to symbolise and really 
epitomise the partnership between central government and local government at the heart 
of decision making. Regenerate Christchurch has four members on its board who are 
appointed by central government, one on the nomination of Te Rūnunga o Ngāi Tahu,

of partnership. The bill as reported back did not give it a big enough role. As a result of 
the negotiations with the Minister and the changes that will be in the Supplementary

12A(3)(c). Those are important changes because only Regenerate Christchurch can now

GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS (WINE AND SPIRITS) REGISTRATION 
AMENDMENT BILL 
First Reading 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH  (Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs) : I 
move, That the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) Registration Amendment 
Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Primary Production Committee to consider 
the bill. This bill amends the Geograph ical Indications (Wines and Spirits) Registration 
Act 2006. A geographical indication is a name —usually a regional name —that is used 
to identify the origin of goods where a quality reputation or other characteristic of the 
goods is related in some essentia l way to their geographical origin. Foreign wine and 
spirit producers use geographical indications to identify their products. Well -known 
examples of these are champagne and Scotch whisky. 
In New Zealand the main user of geographical indications is the loc al wine industry. 
Geographical indications used in New Zealand wines include such terms as 
Marlborough, Martinborough, and Gimblett Gravels. Over time, as an area’s reputation 
grows, the name adds value. New Zealand wines already attract a premium in forei gn 
markets, and we want to preserve that and build on it. 
It is worth taking a moment to reflect on the amazing progress that the New Zealand 
wine industry has had in the last decade or so. It was only in the late 1990s that the New 
Zealand wine exports br oke the $100 million barrier. It is now worth $1.5 billion in 
exports in the last year, and rising fast. That is part of the diverse export economy that 
sustains our living standards here in New Zealand. The Trans -Pacific Partnership, with 
its promise of i mproved market access, is a boost to this industry, and we have heard a 
lot about that over the last few weeks. This bill will also help. 
If I can go and give a bit of background, the World Trade Organization Agreement 
on Trade -related Aspects of Intellect ual Property Rights —otherwise known as the 
TRIPS agreement —obliges New Zealand to provide protection for geographical 
indications for wines and spirits. Geographical indications are currently protected in 
New Zealand by a range of measures, including the t ort of passing off, the Fair Trading 
Act 1986, the Trade Marks Act 2002, and the relevant provisions of the Australia New 
Zealand Food Standards Code. 
The Geographical Indications (Wines and Spirits) Registration Act 2006 provides for 
a registration system of geographical indications, but this Act is not yet in force. It was 
9900 Geo. Indications (Wine & Spirits) Reg. Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2016 
 
passed in anticipation that New Zealand would soon begin negotiations on a wine 
agreement with the European Union. However, negotiations never began. At the time 
the local wine industry  did not have an interest in registering geographical indications, 
so the Act was never brought into force. 
More recently, however, the local wine industry has become concerned about the 
potential misuse of New Zealand geographical indications in export ma rkets. This 
misuse has the potential to adversely affect the reputation of New Zealand wine, which, 
as I have said, commands a premium price in export markets. The further the premium 
grows, the further the potential for misuse increases. The risk can be m itigated by 
registering New Zealand geographical indications in these export markets. However, 
most countries will not register geographical indications unless they are registered in 
their country of origin. As a result, the Government has decided to bring  this Act into 
force. An additional advantage of bringing the Act into force is that it will support New 
Zealand’s interest in launching free-trade agreement negotiations between New Zealand 
and the European Union. 
Before the Act can be brought into force,  some amendments are necessary to clarify 
provisions in the Act and to ensure that the registration process runs smoothly and 
sustainably. These amendments are contained in the amendment bill. Most of these 
amendments are minor and technical. Some amendments are more significant; I will just 
quickly mention these. 
The geographical indication registration expires after 10 years unless a renewal fee is 
paid. The renewal fees will contribute towards the ongoing maintenance of the register 
of geographical indications and help to keep the initial application fees down. 
The second one is that we provide that the terms “New Zealand”, “South Island”, and 
“North Island” will be protected as registered geographical indications without the need 
for an application to be made. These terms are used as geographical indications by local 
wine producers, but might not otherwise meet the definition of “geographical 
indication” in the Act.  
The Registrar of Geographical Indications would be given the power to refuse to 
register a geographical indication if registration or use of the indication would be likely 
to be offensive to a significant section of society, including Māori. This mirrors the 
provision in the Trade Marks Act and ensures that the geographical indications that 
might be refused registration as trademarks on offensiveness grounds cannot be 
registered as geographical indications. 
Once the amendment bill is enacted, the Geographical Indications (Wine and Spirits) 
Registration Act can then be brought into force, and it  will be possible for interested 
parties to apply to register geographical indications. The Act will be administered by the 
Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand, which is also responsible for other 
registered intellectual property rights such as trademarks and patents. 
This is, I think, an important step in the development and maturity of the New 
Zealand wine industry. I hope that it will provide an opportunity to help sustain the 
progress that we are making in this important area of the New  Zealand economy, and it 
is, of course, an important provider of much joy and merriment and happiness to New 
Zealanders and people around the world who enjoy the New Zealand wine in its great 
variety and wonderful, wonderful quality. I do move that this bi ll now be referred to the 
Primary Production Committee for consideration. Thank you.
